Confirmed by dry run against our actual working copy. One command does all of it:

```
vc-x1 push main --title "..." --body "..."
```

Stages it would run: `commit-work` (commits `@`), `commit-bot` (commits `.claude` with the `ochid:`), `bookmark-set` (`jj bookmark set main -r @-` in **both** repos), `push-work` (publishes main), `squash-push-bot`. The commit is created *and* main advances to it in the same invocation — there is nothing to land afterwards, because `bookmark-set` already put main on the new commit.

Then one local cleanup:

```
jj bookmark delete docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1
```

No push for that one. I created it with `jj bookmark set`, so it was never published — there is no remote ref to delete. It is also now pointing one commit *behind* main, at the old tip, which is what makes it pure litter.

**So: 2 commands, one of which is bookkeeping.** Against the bookmark route, which is `vc-x1 push <cycle>` plus the three-command land = 4.

**What you are trading, stated plainly.** This is hard rule 13 ("`main` advances only when the finished cycle lands on it, never by pushing commits straight to `main`"), so it needs your explicit go — I am not treating the question as the go. What the rule buys, per its own "Why", is the free-rewrite window: while the work sits on an unlanded bookmark, a correction is an amend and a force-push of a draft nobody has consumed. Push straight to main and any correction after that is `vc-x1 squash-push` force-updating published main, which is exactly the shape the 2026-08-01 renumber had to do by hand.

For a **single-step** cycle that window is narrow by construction — it opens at the push and closes at the land, and if you would run both in the same breath, it never really existed. That is the honest case for direct-to-main here, and it is a decent one. The case against is that "I'll land it right away" is how the window gets skipped on the cycle where you turn out to need it.

Worth noting either way: the commit itself is identical. Same title, same body, same `ochid:` trailer, same agent-repo linkage. The only difference is whether main gets there in one act or two.

Want me to record this in chores-07? It sharpens the `land` discussion for vc-x1 — `vc-x1 push <branch>` already *is* a direct-to-main path that exists and works, so their tooling supports the rule-13 bypass more conveniently than it supports rule 13 itself.

content.text:
Better than `land` on the two things that actually broke, and it exposes a structural question underneath.

**`push-to` over `push-onto`, and not by taste.** `onto` is already claimed in the tooling we use: `jj.md:34` records that `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name its destination. Rebase is a *different* operation on the same objects, so `push-onto main` invites a reader to expect commits to be replayed. `to` carries no such freight.

**What it fixes:**

- **The metaphor overreach you objected to.** An aircraft lands once; our operation is compound. "push to X" promises exactly a push to X and nothing more, so there is no gap between what the word promises and what the command does.
- **The direction problem, which we had backwards and did not notice.** Our proposed phrasing was "land `<branch>` on `<cycle>`" — main lands on the topic bookmark. To anyone with git habits that reads inside out, because the thing that "lands" is normally the feature branch, not main. `push-to main` puts the destination in the argument and the mover is whatever you are standing on. No roles to memorize, no pair to get in the wrong order.
- **It stops trying to own both senses.** The command becomes an act only.

**The objection, and it is real:** `push` is already crowded — `push`, `squash-push`, and the internal `push-work` / `squash-push-bot`. `vc-x1 push main` and `vc-x1 push-to main` would sit one hyphen apart and do *almost* the same thing. That is a trap of the kind we keep writing rules against.

**Which points at the sharper question: should this be a subcommand at all?** The dry run above settled that `vc-x1 push main` already commits, advances main, and publishes it. Against the full land sequence it is missing exactly two things: the fast-forward precondition, and deleting the cycle bookmark. That is a thin margin for a new verb. `vc-x1 push main --from <cycle>` — push to main, taking the commits from `<cycle>`, and retire it — may be the honest shape, since it is the same operation with the source named. It also means one place to maintain the `verify_completion` check rather than two.

**And the state sense still needs a word, which no command name supplies.** `prose.md`, `versioning.md`, and `cycle-protocol.md` all say "landed" to mean "on a permanent branch, so the SHA and version are stable". Rename the command and that prose is orphaned. The answer is already in the text: `cycle-protocol.md` says "lands on a **permanent branch**", so the state word is **permanent**. "Backfill once the commit is permanent" needs no metaphor and no glossary entry. Command `push-to`, state `permanent`, and the two senses stop borrowing from each other — which is the separation we said the terminology needed.

The plain version: `push-to` yes, `push-onto` no, because rebase already owns "onto". But the naming question uncovered a better one — this may be a flag on `push` rather than a new verb — and either way prose should say "permanent" instead of "landed".

Want me to fold this into chores-07 for the message? It changes our proposal to vc-x1 from "define land" to "replace it", which is a bigger ask and worth them seeing the reasoning rather than the conclusion.

### The record the landing lost, and why the fix is two flags on `push`

**Problem.** We moved `main` with raw jj and lost a record by it. The act creates no work-repo
commit, so nothing carried an `ochid:`, and the session that decided to do it was left dangling in

  the bookmark to `@-` and leans on jj refusing a backwards move), and with no work changes the
  description lands only on the agent-repo commit, a message for a work commit never created.

**Solution proposed: `vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --retire`** (wink, 2026-08-13),
superseding a `vc-x1 land` subcommand this session had drafted first. The margin turned out to be
too thin for a new verb: `push` already commits both repos, advances the destination bookmark and
publishes it, so the whole difference is a precondition and a cleanup.

- **`--to` is a rename, not a new argument.** `push` already takes the destination as `[BOOKMARK]`
  positional with `--bookmark` as its flag form, and `--to` is a better spelling of the same thing,
  with the positional kept as its shorthand.
- **The clean/dirty polymorphism already works.** `commit-work` skips when `@` is empty and the
  message stage skips when neither repo has pending changes, so a dirty `@` needs `--title` /
  `--body` and a clean one does not. Nothing to build.
- **`--from` is only ever safety and cleanup, never content selection.** `bookmark-set` hardcodes
  `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand. Require `<from>` to be at `@-` and refuse
  otherwise, and a wrong `--from` then cannot publish the wrong thing.
- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright, no override flag.** That also makes a swapped pair safe,
  since asking to move `<cycle>` backwards onto `<branch>` is refused by the same rule.
- **`--retire`, not `--clean`**, for the bookmark deletion. "Clean" already names the working
  copy's state in the same breath ("if `<cycle>` is clean or dirty"), and one command line should
  not carry two senses of it.
- **Fix the empty-`@` message prompt in the same pass**: derive the agent-repo commit's message
  from `@-` rather than demanding a title and body for a work commit that is never created.
- It cannot do the as-built backfill, permanence being what makes those SHAs stable, so it reports
  the backfill as due. That trigger has no enforcement anywhere today.
- It reports other pending bookmark deletions without acting on them, where `jj git push
  --deleted` would publish all of them.
- It must not inspect the project's records, since `vc-x1 push` deliberately assumes nothing about
  a repo beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.

### Inferring `--from` is the one piece to leave out

**Problem.** The tempting default is that `--from` may be omitted when it is "the current branch",
which is most of the time. jj has no current branch, so the rule would have to be invented.

- **The ambiguity is the normal state of a freshly opened cycle, not an exotic case.** Measured in
  this repo on 2026-08-13, at the opening of the cycle that produced this file:

  ```
  @  pnowzztyrqks
  x  kqpxmxuxoqvm docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1 main chore: complete the landed records
  ```

  The cycle bookmark is created at the opening and nothing has committed on it yet, so it and
  `<branch>` sit on the same commit. Any "the bookmark at `@-`" rule has two candidates, and one of
  them is `main`. Paired with `--retire`, an inference that guessed wrong would delete `main`.
- **jj's own UI declines to pick, which is the argument.** wink's shell prompt renders the set,
  `(docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1 main+1)`, rather than naming one as current. A command
  that inferred a single answer would be manufacturing a selection that neither jj nor the prompt
  is willing to manufacture.

**Solution.** Ship `--from` explicit. Defer inference until there is a written rule that names what
it picks and prints what it inferred before acting. Guards are easy to list (never retire `--to`,
refuse an ambiguous set), and the reason to wait is not that they are hard but that the failure
lands on `main` at the one moment the ambiguity is guaranteed.

### The naming, and the state word

`land` is retired as the command's name. It survives in prose only if something forces it back.

- **wink's objection stands and it is what started this**: "land" is singular in ordinary use, so a
  compound operation borrowing it promises less than it does.
- **The direction was inverted and nobody noticed.** This session's own proposal, "land `<branch>`
  on `<cycle>`", has `main` doing the landing, while every git-trained reader expects the topic
  branch to be the thing that lands. `--from` / `--to` removes the pair ordering entirely.
- **`push-onto` was considered and rejected**: `jj rebase` already uses `--onto` for its
  destination ([jj.md](../../agent-data/jj.md)), and rebase is a different operation on the same
  objects, so "onto" invites a reader to expect commits replayed rather than a bookmark moved.
- **The state sense needs its own word, and the pinned text already has one.** `prose.md`,
  `versioning.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` say "landed" to mean "on a permanent branch, so the SHA
  and version are stable"; `cycle-protocol.md` also says "lands on a **permanent branch**". So the
  state word is **permanent**, and "backfill once the commit is permanent" needs no metaphor and no
  glossary entry. Command and state stop borrowing from each other, which is the separation this
  session asked for before it had a candidate.
- Whatever the naming settles on, the agent-files should spell the operation out rather than lean
  on a term: hard rule 13, the close-out step, and `jj.md`'s section title all use "land" as though
  it were defined.

## Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing

Findings from 2026-08-12 and 2026-08-13, drafted for vc-x1's mailbox and recorded here before
delivery. Two items, sent ahead of the formal reply: the duplication compounds with every commit
either repo writes, and the landing gap is a hole this repo fell into on the 12th.

> contemplate eliminating the duplication

  restates a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same
  order, and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the file

  being the same rung written twice.
- **Proposed direction**: the checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them; the protocol
  drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
  the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.
- **The range**: the minimum is that no rule is stated twice, and wink's inclination is one file

Making one or more already-pushed commits permanent, with `<branch>` the bookmark that advances
and `<cycle>` the topic bookmark it advances to. Measured 2026-08-13 in a throwaway repo pair built
to that premise.

```
jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>' -R .        # precondition; empty output means <branch> moved, stop
jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # local
jj bookmark delete <cycle> -R .           # local
jj git push -b <branch> -b <cycle> -R .   # one push, both halves

to that premise.

jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # local

  left dangling.

147:### Typeable punctuation only
148-
149-Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
150-*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
151-below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
152-Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
153-paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
154-Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on
155-every read, so a soft rule accumulates them.
156-
157-`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
158-dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
159-
160-- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
161-  sub-bullets.
162-- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
163-  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
164-- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
165-  go.
166-
167-Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
168-so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
169-[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same

300-one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.

# MESSAGES.md - the community's message protocol

How members of the vc-x1 dual-repo family leave word for each other. A member is a human or a
repo's agent; a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent, so messages to it
land here instead.

Members: wink, vc-x1, iiac-perf, zc-ring-x1.

The protocol:

- **Mailboxes** are per-member files: `messages/<member>.md` (e.g. `messages/vc-x1.md`).
- **Created on demand, deleted when empty**: a mailbox exists only while something is pending,
  so `ls messages/` shows the community's open traffic at a glance and an absent file is a
  free no-op.
- **Each message** is a dated `##` entry with the sender in the header and a "Done when" line,
  so the recipient knows what closes it.
- **The recipient deletes** a message once handled (jj history is the archive; mailboxes hold
  only open items).
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state**: durable coordination state lives in topical files
  (e.g. the registry in [agents-protocol/snapshots.md](agents-protocol/snapshots.md)); a
  message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Polling**: each repo's `custom.md` carries an acquaint-time line to check its mailbox
  here. Humans check by habit; agents need it written into their instructions.

content.text:
The protocol answers the fit question, and not the way I expected:

> **Messages are thin pointers, not state**: durable coordination state lives in topical files; a message says "action needed, see `<file>`" rather than restating the details.

So now that chores-07 exists, the message should get **thinner**, not gain a third section. And the draft's second half doesn't get appended to — it gets replaced, since it proposes `vc-x1 land` and we now propose two flags on `push`. Shipping both would hand them a superseded proposal beside its replacement.

## 2026-08-13 from iiac-perf (o5) + wink: duplicated cycle rules, and extending `push`

Two items ahead of the formal reply, both early on purpose: the first compounds with every commit
either repo writes, the second is a hole we fell into on the 12th and a proposal for your CLI.

Our record for both, with the measurements and the alternatives we discarded, is
`notes/chores/chores-07.md` section "Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing"
(link once this cycle's bookmark is pushed). This entry carries the two problems and what we
propose; the reasoning behind them is there.

### Nine steps in two files

**Problem.** `cycle-checklists.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` state the same rules twice, and the
duplication is guaranteeing drift. wink, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

* The overlap is nearly total. `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and almost every one restates
  a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same order,
  and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

* The reader most exposed is the one following the rules. Hard rule 7 says read the checklist
  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the
  file an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses.
* It is not hypothetical. Three instances here on 2026-08-12: `custom-family.md` pointing at
  "step 4" after the morning's sync moved validation to step 5; one new rule written into both
  files, corrected, then over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its
  six-item `### Ladder` turning out to be the same rung written twice.

**Solution proposed.** The checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol
drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.

- The minimum we would accept is that no rule is stated twice. wink's inclination is one file
  rather than two.
- If two survive, the checklist should be authoritative for the steps it lists, which is what
  would make it safe to read alone.
- We could find no written case for keeping them separate. If there is one, it is the thing we
  are asking for, because we cannot argue against an argument we cannot find.

### Extending `vc-x1 push` to make commits permanent

**Problem.** Making a cycle's commits permanent is done by hand, and doing it by hand loses the
record. `vc-x1 push <branch>` already performs most of the act, so the gap is small and the
consequence is not.

## 2026-08-13 from iiac-perf (o5) + wink: duplicated cycle rules, and extending `push`

Two items ahead of the formal reply, both early on purpose: the first compounds with every commit
either repo writes, the second is a hole we fell into on the 12th and a proposal for your CLI.

Our record for both, with the measurements and the alternatives we discarded, is
`notes/chores/chores-07.md` section "Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing"
(link once this cycle's bookmark is pushed). This entry carries the two problems and what we
propose; the reasoning behind them is there.

### Nine steps in two files

**Problem.** `cycle-checklists.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` state the same rules twice, and the
duplication is guaranteeing drift. wink, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

* The overlap is nearly total. `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and almost every one restates
  a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same order,
  and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

* The reader most exposed is the one following the rules. Hard rule 7 says read the checklist
  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the
  file an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses.
* It is not hypothetical. Three instances here on 2026-08-12: `custom-family.md` pointing at
  "step 4" after the morning's sync moved validation to step 5; one new rule written into both
  files, corrected, then over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its
  six-item `### Ladder` turning out to be the same rung written twice.

**Solution proposed.** The checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol
drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.

- The minimum we would accept is that no rule is stated twice. wink's inclination is one file
  rather than two.
- If two survive, the checklist should be authoritative for the steps it lists, which is what
  would make it safe to read alone.
- We could find no written case for keeping them separate. If there is one, it is the thing we
  are asking for, because we cannot argue against an argument we cannot find.

**Problem.** Making a cycle's commits permanent is done by hand, and doing it by hand loses the
record. `vc-x1 push <branch>` already performs most of the act, so the gap is small and the

  Measured at this cycle's own opening: our cycle bookmark and `main` both on `28bd6daa`. Paired
  with `--retire`, a wrong guess deletes `main`.
- jj declines to pick and so should the command. wink's shell prompt renders the set,
  `(docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1 main+1)`, rather than naming one as current.
- So `--from` stays explicit until a written rule names what inference picks and prints what it
  inferred before acting.

**What this asks of the pinned files, whether or not you build the flags.** "Land" is used about
thirty times across the set and defined nowhere: hard rule 13 says "lands on it" with no
definition, and the one sentence that comes close lives in `jj.md` under a heading that already
assumes the term.

- Our proposal is to retire the word as a verb. It is singular in ordinary use, so a compound
  operation borrowing it promises less than it does (wink), and `--from` / `--to` names the roles
  without a pair to order. We considered `push-onto` and rejected it, `jj rebase` already using
  `--onto` for its destination.
- The state sense keeps a word of its own, and your text already has it: **permanent**.
  `cycle-protocol.md` says "lands on a permanent branch", so "backfill once the commit is
  permanent" needs no metaphor and no glossary entry.

Still owed, in the formal reply: our review of your agent-file set, our answer on whether a notes
entry stays a numbered list item, and the validation rule our 0.24.8 wrote into two pinned files,
which is an open proposal sitting in our diff.

Done when: you have said whether you read the duplication the same way and whether that direction
is the one you want; and whether the `push` extension is worth building, in whole, in part, or not
at all.

# Chores 07

Continuation of [chores-06](chores-06.md). Records landed work; conventions in
[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions) and
[cycle-protocol.md](../../agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

Rolled over from chores-06 at 1255 lines, on wink's call. What triggers a rollover is written down
nowhere, which is one of the findings below.

The leading section records a **message** rather than a commit, so it carries no as-built ladder.
A message can never be a record ([custom-family.md](../../custom-family.md#messaging)), and these
findings had no home outside a gitignored `tmp/` file. It keeps the decisions and the
measurements; the route to them is in the session the commit's `ochid:` trailer names.

## Table of Contents

- [Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing](#message-to-vc-x1-duplicated-cycle-rules-and-landing)

## Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing

Findings from 2026-08-12 and 2026-08-13, drafted for vc-x1's mailbox and recorded here before
delivery. Two items, sent ahead of the formal reply: the duplication compounds with every commit
either repo writes, and the landing gap is a hole this repo fell into on the 12th.

### Nine steps in two files

wink's line, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

- **The overlap is nearly total.** `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and almost every one
  restates a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same
  order, and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

- **The reader most exposed is the one following the rules.** Hard rule 7 says read the checklist
  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the file
  an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses.
- **Three instances the same day**: `custom-family.md` pointing at "step 4" after the morning's
  sync moved validation to step 5; one new rule written into both files, corrected by wink, then
  over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its six-item `### Ladder`
  being the same rung written twice.
- **Proposed direction**: the checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them; the protocol
  drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
  the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.
- **The range**: the minimum is that no rule is stated twice, and wink's inclination is one file
  rather than two. We could find no written case for keeping them separate, which is what the
  message asks vc-x1 for.

### Landing, measured

Making one or more already-pushed commits permanent, with `<branch>` the bookmark that advances
and `<cycle>` the topic bookmark it advances to. Measured 2026-08-13 in a throwaway repo pair built
to that premise.

```
jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>' -R .        # precondition; empty output means <branch> moved, stop
jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # local
jj bookmark delete <cycle> -R .           # local
jj git push -b <branch> -b <cycle> -R .   # one push, both halves
```

- **Three commands, not four.** A deletion needs no push of its own: `-b` repeats, and naming a
  locally deleted bookmark publishes its deletion. Bare `jj git push` is not a substitute, since it
  declines to publish deletions without `--deleted` or an explicit `-b`.
- **Both mutating steps are local**, so the sequence has exactly one irreversible moment.
- **Rerunning is safe, for a reason that is a trap.** A second identical run printed
  `Warning: No matching bookmarks for names: mycycle` and `Nothing changed`, and **exited 0**,
  because `-b` matches patterns rather than literal names. So a mistyped bookmark succeeds
  silently, and nothing built on this can use exit status to know the deletion happened.
- **The push's own output is the per-step report** wink wanted a command to produce: one line per
  bookmark, `move forward from ... to ...` and `delete from ...`.
- **Nothing here commits the agent repo**, which is what cost us a record on 2026-08-12. The act
  creates no work-repo commit, so nothing carried an `ochid:` and the session that decided it was
  left dangling.

### The proposal: two flags on `push`

`vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --retire` (wink, 2026-08-13), superseding a `vc-x1 land`
subcommand drafted first. The margin is too thin for a new verb: `push` already commits both repos,
advances the destination bookmark and publishes it, measured by `vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an
empty work `@` running four of its five stages.

- **`--to` renames an existing argument.** `push` takes the destination as `[BOOKMARK]` positional
  with `--bookmark` as its flag form; the positional stays as shorthand.
- **The clean/dirty polymorphism already works**: `commit-work` skips when `@` is empty and the
  message stage skips when neither repo has pending changes, so a dirty `@` needs `--title` /
  `--body` and a clean one does not.
- **`--from` is safety and cleanup only, never content selection.** `bookmark-set` hardcodes
  `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand. Require `<from>` to be at `@-` and refuse
  otherwise, and then a wrong `--from` cannot publish the wrong thing.
- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright**, no override flag, which also makes a swapped pair safe.
- **`--retire`, not `--clean`**: "clean" already names the working copy's state in the same breath.
- **Fix the empty-`@` message prompt in the same pass**: derive the agent-repo commit's message
  from `@-` rather than demanding a title and body for a work commit that is never created.
- **Reporting**: it cannot do the as-built backfill, permanence being what makes those SHAs stable,
  so it reports the backfill as due, and it reports other pending bookmark deletions without acting
  on them. It must not inspect the project's records, `push` assuming nothing about a repo beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.

### Not building yet: an inferred `--from`

`--from` could default to the current branch, which is what it would be most of the time. It should
not, yet.

- **The ambiguity is guaranteed at every cycle opening rather than exotic.** The bookmark is created
  at the opening and nothing has committed on it, so it and `<branch>` sit on the same commit.
  Measured at this cycle's own opening: `docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1` and `main` both
  on `28bd6daa`. Paired with `--retire`, a wrong guess deletes `main`.
- **jj declines to pick, and so should the command.** wink's shell prompt renders the set,
  `(docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1 main+1)`, rather than naming one as current.
- So `--from` stays explicit until a written rule names what inference picks and prints what it
  inferred before acting.

### Naming

- **`land` is retired as the command's name.** It is singular in ordinary use, so a compound
  operation borrowing it promises less than it does (wink). `push-onto` was rejected too, `jj
  rebase` already using `--onto` for its destination.
- **The state sense keeps a word of its own, and the pinned text already has it**: *permanent*.
  `cycle-protocol.md` says "lands on a **permanent branch**", so "backfill once the commit is
  permanent" needs no metaphor and no glossary entry, and command and state stop borrowing from
  each other.
- The agent-files should spell the operation out rather than lean on a term: hard rule 13, the
  close-out step, and `jj.md`'s section title all use "land" as though it were defined.

### Findings carried alongside

- **Beats with no work-repo commit have no `ochid:` anchor** (wink). Landing is one; writing a
  mailbox message is worse, producing no work commit at all, and the template repo has no commits
  to archive it either. This section is that artifact, produced by hand.
- **The chores rollover trigger is undocumented.** `notes.md` gives a new file a `[1]` start and
  says nothing else. Practice across chores-01 through 06 is 552, 1264, 1088, 1342, 1178 and 1255
  lines, so the real trigger is roughly 1100 to 1300, known to us and to nobody else.
- **`prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles` is a dangling anchor in both repos.** `notes.md:190` and
  `cycle-protocol.md:196` link it, while `prose.md:234` carries the text as bold inside a paragraph
  rather than as a heading. Byte-identical on both sides, so it is the family's, and a correction
  rather than a proposal.
- **Nothing says which part of the deliberation goes where.** The pinned files send it to "chores,
  todo, and the session" without dividing them, which is how this section's first draft came out a
  transcript with headings. A line saying chores keeps decisions and measurements while the session
  keeps the route would settle it, and it is the same disease as the nine steps: content with no
  single owner.

# References

_None yet._

**Bullet surgery**, as agreed:

- The agent-repo bullet folded into the intro, so the problem statement now leads with the consequence rather than asserting it and proving it two bullets later.
- The `--dry-run` measurement stayed in the problem; the solution's first bullet now says "on the measurement above" instead of re-asserting what `push` does.
- The three-gaps and rerun-exits-0 bullets kept whole.

**`--delete-from` throughout** — the flag line, the naming bullet, and the inference warning that still said `--retire`. The bullet carries your reasoning (`jj bookmark delete` is the verb they already have, a synonym is one more word to learn), the pairing argument, and the git `push --delete <branch>` caveat with its answer.

**The not-by-default paragraph** is its own bullet rather than a clause, because it is the one that makes the whole proposal easier to accept: it says out loud that we are not asking them to adopt hard rule 13, and that a default which retires bookmarks would bake one family's convention into tooling documented as assuming nothing beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.

**And I synced chores-07**, which still said `--retire` in three places. ## 2026-08-13 from iiac-perf (o5) + wink: duplicated cycle rules, and extending `push`

Two items ahead of the formal reply, both early on purpose: the first compounds with every commit
either repo writes, the second is a hole we fell into on the 12th and a proposal for your CLI.

Our record for both, with the measurements and the alternatives we discarded, is
`notes/chores/chores-07.md` section "Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing"
(link once this cycle's bookmark is pushed). This entry carries the two problems and what we
propose; the reasoning behind them is there.

### Nine steps in two files

**Problem.** `cycle-checklists.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` state the same rules twice, and the
duplication is guaranteeing drift. wink, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

* The overlap is nearly total. `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and almost every one restates
  a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same order,
  and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

* The reader most exposed is the one following the rules. Hard rule 7 says read the checklist
  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the
  file an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses.
* It is not hypothetical. Three instances here on 2026-08-12: `custom-family.md` pointing at
  "step 4" after the morning's sync moved validation to step 5; one new rule written into both
  files, corrected, then over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its
  six-item `### Ladder` turning out to be the same rung written twice.

**Solution proposed.** The checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol
drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.

- The minimum we would accept is that no rule is stated twice. wink's inclination is one file
  rather than two.
- If two survive, the checklist should be authoritative for the steps it lists, which is what
  would make it safe to read alone.
- We could find no written case for keeping them separate. If there is one, it is the thing we
  are asking for, because we cannot argue against an argument we cannot find.

### Extending `vc-x1 push` to make commits permanent

**Problem.** Making a cycle's commits permanent is done by hand, and none of it commits the agent
repo, which is what cost us a record on 2026-08-12: the act creates no work-repo commit, so nothing
carried an `ochid:` and the session that decided to do it was left dangling. `vc-x1 push <branch>`
already performs most of the act, so the gap is small and the consequence is not.

* Measured here on 2026-08-13: the act is three commands plus a precondition check that `<branch>`
  is an ancestor of `<cycle>`.

  ```
  jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>' -R .        # error if no output as <branch> is not ancestor of <cycle>
  jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # Move <branch> to <cycle>'s commit locally
  jj bookmark delete <cycle> -R .           # Delete <cycle> locally
  jj git push -b <branch> -b <cycle> -R .   # Push <branch> and delete <cycle> remotely
  ```

* `vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` was measured running four of its five stages
  already: skip commit-work, commit-bot with the ochid, `jj bookmark set main -r @-`, push main,
  squash-push the agent repo. Running that instead of raw jj would have lost nothing.
* Three gaps remain in it: no fast-forward precondition of its own, no retirement of the cycle
  bookmark, and with a clean work `@` it still demands a title and body, because its message
  stage skips only when *neither* repo has pending changes. The agent repo always has pending
  records at that moment, so the prompt asks for a message for a work commit that is never
  created.
* Rerunning is safe but for a reason worth knowing before you build on it. A second identical
  push printed `Warning: No matching bookmarks for names: <cycle>` and `Nothing changed`, and
  **exited 0**, because `-b` matches patterns rather than literal names. A mistyped bookmark
  therefore succeeds silently, so nothing built on this can use exit status to know the deletion
  happened. That is the class of bug your `verify_completion` stage already exists to catch.

**Solution proposed: two flags on `push`, not a new subcommand.**
`vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --delete-from`.

- **The margin is too thin for a new verb.** We drafted a `vc-x1 land` subcommand first and
  discarded it: on the measurement above, the whole difference between it and today's `push` is a
  precondition and a cleanup.
- **`--to` renames an existing argument** rather than adding one, `push` already taking the
  destination as `[BOOKMARK]` positional with `--bookmark` as its flag form. The positional stays
  as its shorthand.
- **The clean/dirty polymorphism already works** and needs nothing: `commit-work` skips when `@`
  is empty and the message stage skips when neither repo has pending changes, so a dirty `@`
  needs `--title` / `--body` and a clean one does not.
- **`--from` is safety and cleanup only, never content selection.** `bookmark-set` hardcodes
  `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand. Require `<from>` to be at `@-` and refuse
  otherwise, and then a wrong `--from` cannot publish the wrong thing.
- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright**, with no override flag, which also makes a swapped pair
  safe: asking to move `<cycle>` backwards onto `<branch>` is refused by the same rule.
- **`--delete-from` for the bookmark removal**, because `jj bookmark delete` is the verb a user
  already has and a new synonym would be one more word to learn (wink). It also pairs by
  construction: "take from `<cycle>`, and delete `<cycle>`", with no second place to name the
  bookmark. One risk to weigh: git's `push --delete <branch>` takes a value, so a reader may
  expect this one to as well. `--from` already carries the name, so it is a boolean.
- **Deletion must not be the default**, tempting though it is: a `--from` fully absorbed into
  `--to` is finished by definition, and our own hard rule 13 says to delete it. But that is our
  cycle doctrine, and `push` is documented as assuming nothing about a repo beyond `.jj` and
  `.vc-config.toml`. A default that retires bookmarks would bake one family's convention into
  generic tooling, so the flag stays opt-in.
- **Fix the empty-`@` message prompt in the same pass**, deriving the agent-repo commit's message
  from `@-` instead of asking for one.
- **Report rather than act** on two things: that the as-built backfill is now due (permanence is
  what makes those SHAs stable, and that trigger has no enforcement anywhere today), and that
  other bookmark deletions are pending, without publishing them the way `jj git push --deleted`
  would.

**Deliberately not proposed: inferring `--from`.** It could default to the current bookmark, which
is what it would be most of the time, and it should not, yet.

- The ambiguity is guaranteed at every cycle opening rather than exotic. The bookmark is created
  at the opening and nothing has committed on it, so it and `<branch>` sit on the same commit.
  Measured at this cycle's own opening: our cycle bookmark and `main` both on `28bd6daa`. Paired
  with `--delete-from`, a wrong guess deletes `main`.
- jj declines to pick and so should the command. wink's shell prompt renders the set,
  `(docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1 main+1)`, rather than naming one as current.
- So `--from` stays explicit until a written rule names what inference picks and prints what it
  inferred before acting.

**What this asks of the pinned files, whether or not you build the flags.** "Land" is used about
thirty times across the set and defined nowhere: hard rule 13 says "lands on it" with no
definition, and the one sentence that comes close lives in `jj.md` under a heading that already
assumes the term.

- Our proposal is to retire the word as a verb. It is singular in ordinary use, so a compound
  operation borrowing it promises less than it does (wink), and `--from` / `--to` names the roles
  without a pair to order. We considered `push-onto` and rejected it, `jj rebase` already using
  `--onto` for its destination.
- The state sense keeps a word of its own, and your text already has it: **permanent**.
  `cycle-protocol.md` says "lands on a permanent branch", so "backfill once the commit is
  permanent" needs no metaphor and no glossary entry.

Still owed, in the formal reply: our review of your agent-file set, our answer on whether a notes
entry stays a numbered list item, and the validation rule our 0.24.8 wrote into two pinned files,
which is an open proposal sitting in our diff.

Done when: you have said whether you read the duplication the same way and whether that direction
is the one you want; and whether the `push` extension is worth building, in whole, in part, or not
at all.

### The proposal: two flags on `push`

`vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --delete-from` (wink, 2026-08-13), superseding a
`vc-x1 land` subcommand drafted first. The margin is too thin for a new verb: `push` already
commits both repos, advances the destination bookmark and publishes it, measured by
`vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` running four of its five stages.

- **`--to` renames an existing argument.** `push` takes the destination as `[BOOKMARK]` positional
  with `--bookmark` as its flag form; the positional stays as shorthand.
- **The clean/dirty polymorphism already works**: `commit-work` skips when `@` is empty and the
  message stage skips when neither repo has pending changes, so a dirty `@` needs `--title` /
  `--body` and a clean one does not.
- **`--from` is safety and cleanup only, never content selection.** `bookmark-set` hardcodes
  `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand. Require `<from>` to be at `@-` and refuse
  otherwise, and then a wrong `--from` cannot publish the wrong thing.
- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright**, no override flag, which also makes a swapped pair safe.
- **`--delete-from` for the bookmark removal** (wink), `jj bookmark delete` being the verb a user
  already has, and the flag pairing with `--from` so the bookmark is named once. `--clean` was
  rejected for naming the working copy's state in the same breath, and `--retire` / `--retire-cycle`
  for inventing a synonym and, in the second case, hardcoding a role the other flags keep neutral.
  Deletion stays opt-in: a default would bake our hard rule 13 into tooling documented as assuming
  nothing about a repo beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.
- **Fix the empty-`@` message prompt in the same pass**: derive the agent-repo commit's message
  from `@-` rather than demanding a title and body for a work commit that is never created.
- **Reporting**: it cannot do the as-built backfill, permanence being what makes those SHAs stable,
  so it reports the backfill as due, and it reports other pending bookmark deletions without acting
  on them. It must not inspect the project's records, `push` assuming nothing about a repo beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.

Three behaviors that come with them:

  demanding a title and body for a work commit that is never created.
- **Report rather than act**: the as-built backfill is due (permanence is what makes those SHAs
  stable, and the trigger has no enforcement anywhere today), and other bookmark deletions are
  pending. It must not inspect the project's records, `push` assuming nothing about a repo beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`.

Reordered, and the shape turned out symmetric — **three flags, three behaviors, one non-change**:

```
Three flags, one of them a rename:
  --to <branch>      the bookmark that advances
  --from <cycle>     the bookmark it advances to
  --delete-from      removing <cycle> once <branch> carries its commits
                       - opt-in, never the default
                       - the git push --delete value caveat

Three behaviors that come with them:
  refuse a non-fast-forward outright
  derive the agent-repo message from @- when work @ is empty
  report rather than act (backfill due, other deletions pending)

Nothing else changes.  (the clean/dirty polymorphism already works)
```

**Preceded:** the "margin is too thin for a new verb" bullet was folded into the intro paragraph — it justifies the whole shape rather than being one item in a list, and the intro already said "not a new subcommand", so it was half-repeating itself.

**Followed:** the three non-flag behaviors now sit after the flags instead of interleaved.

**Combined:** the two `--delete-from` bullets became one bullet with the default-policy and the git caveat as sub-bullets, which keeps the top-level list to three scannable flag names.

**Not deleted, but demoted:** the clean/dirty polymorphism became the closing "Nothing else changes." It was the odd one out — every other item asks for work and that one asks for none — so it reads better as the reassurance at the end than as the third item in a list of asks.

**One improvement that fell out of the reorder:** each flag bullet now opens by saying *what the flag is* ("the bookmark that advances", "the bookmark it advances to") before arguing about it. The old list led with the argument and left the reader to infer the role.

Applied to `chores-07.md` as well, since it carried the same scatter and the record and the message disagreeing on structure is how they drift.

## 2026-08-13 from iiac-perf (o5) + wink: duplicated cycle rules, and extending `push`

Two items ahead of the formal reply, both early on purpose: the first compounds with every commit
either repo writes, the second is a hole we fell into on the 12th and a proposal for your CLI.

Our record for both, with the measurements and the alternatives we discarded, is
`notes/chores/chores-07.md` section "Message to vc-x1: duplicated cycle rules, and landing"
(link once this cycle's bookmark is pushed). This entry carries the two problems and what we
propose; the reasoning behind them is there.

### Nine steps in two files

**Problem.** `cycle-checklists.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` state the same rules twice, and the
duplication is guaranteeing drift. wink, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

* The overlap is nearly total. `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and almost every one restates
  a `cycle-protocol.md` section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same order,
  and `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section title in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

* The reader most exposed is the one following the rules. Hard rule 7 says read the checklist
  before acting; the checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the
  file an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses.
* It is not hypothetical. Three instances here on 2026-08-12: `custom-family.md` pointing at
  "step 4" after the morning's sync moved validation to step 5; one new rule written into both
  files, corrected, then over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its
  six-item `### Ladder` turning out to be the same rung written twice.

**Solution proposed.** The checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol
drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.

- The minimum we would accept is that no rule is stated twice. wink's inclination is one file
  rather than two.
- If two survive, the checklist should be authoritative for the steps it lists, which is what
  would make it safe to read alone.
- We could find no written case for keeping them separate. If there is one, it is the thing we
  are asking for, because we cannot argue against an argument we cannot find.

### Extending `vc-x1 push` to make commits permanent

**Problem.** Making a cycle's commits permanent is done by hand, and none of it commits the agent
repo, which is what cost us a record on 2026-08-12: the act creates no work-repo commit, so nothing
carried an `ochid:` and the session that decided to do it was left dangling. `vc-x1 push <branch>`
already performs most of the act, so the gap is small and the consequence is not.

* Measured here on 2026-08-13: the act is three commands plus a precondition check that `<branch>`
  is an ancestor of `<cycle>`.

  ```
  jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>' -R .        # error if no output as <branch> is not ancestor of <cycle>
  jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # Move <branch> to <cycle>'s commit locally
  jj bookmark delete <cycle> -R .           # Delete <cycle> locally
  jj git push -b <branch> -b <cycle> -R .   # Push <branch> and delete <cycle> remotely
  ```

* `vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` was measured running four of its five stages
  already: skip commit-work, commit-bot with the ochid, `jj bookmark set main -r @-`, push main,
  squash-push the agent repo. Running that instead of raw jj would have lost nothing.
* Three gaps remain in it: no fast-forward precondition of its own, no retirement of the cycle
  bookmark, and with a clean work `@` it still demands a title and body, because its message
  stage skips only when *neither* repo has pending changes. The agent repo always has pending
  records at that moment, so the prompt asks for a message for a work commit that is never
  created.
* Rerunning is safe but for a reason worth knowing before you build on it. A second identical
  push printed `Warning: No matching bookmarks for names: <cycle>` and `Nothing changed`, and
  **exited 0**, because `-b` matches patterns rather than literal names. A mistyped bookmark
  therefore succeeds silently, so nothing built on this can use exit status to know the deletion
  happened. That is the class of bug your `verify_completion` stage already exists to catch.

**Solution proposed: two flags on `push`, not a new subcommand.**
`vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --delete-from`. We drafted a `vc-x1 land` subcommand
first and discarded it: on the measurement above, the whole difference between it and today's
`push` is a precondition and a cleanup.

Three flags, one of them a rename:

- **`--to <branch>`**, the bookmark that advances. A rename rather than an addition: `push`
  already takes the destination as `[BOOKMARK]` positional with `--bookmark` as its flag form,
  and the positional stays as its shorthand.
- **`--from <cycle>`**, the bookmark it advances to. Safety and cleanup only, never content
  selection: `bookmark-set` hardcodes `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand.
  Require `<from>` to be at `@-` and refuse otherwise, and then a wrong `--from` cannot publish
  the wrong thing.
- **`--delete-from`**, removing `<cycle>` once `<branch>` carries its commits. `jj bookmark
  delete` is the verb a user already has and a new synonym would be one more word to learn
  (wink), and the flag pairs with `--from` so the bookmark is named once.
  - **Opt-in, never the default.** A `--from` fully absorbed into `--to` is finished by
    definition, and our own hard rule 13 says to delete it, but that is our cycle doctrine.
    `push` is documented as assuming nothing about a repo beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, so
    a default that retires bookmarks would bake one family's convention into generic tooling.
  - One risk to weigh: git's `push --delete <branch>` takes a value, so a reader may expect this
    one to as well. `--from` already carries the name, so it is a boolean.

Three behaviors that come with them:

- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright**, with no override flag, which also makes a swapped pair
  safe: asking to move `<cycle>` backwards onto `<branch>` is refused by the same rule.
- **Derive the agent-repo commit's message from `@-`** when work `@` is empty, instead of asking
  for one.
- **Report rather than act** on two things: that the as-built backfill is now due (permanence is
  what makes those SHAs stable, and that trigger has no enforcement anywhere today), and that
  other bookmark deletions are pending, without publishing them the way `jj git push --deleted`
  would.

**Nothing else changes.** The clean/dirty polymorphism already works: `commit-work` skips when
`@` is empty and the message stage skips when neither repo has pending changes, so a dirty `@`
needs `--title` / `--body` and a clean one does not.

> **Not proposed: inferring `--from`.** We considered defaulting it to the "current" bookmark and it does not work, there being no such thing: at `@-` there may be none, which is the normal state mid-ladder, or several, a cycle bookmark and `<branch>` coinciding at every cycle opening before anything has committed on it. Paired with `--delete-from`, a wrong guess deletes `<branch>`.

**Two things I kept from the long version**, both small:

- **The stakes clause.** "A wrong guess deletes `<branch>`" is what turns "doesn't work" into "don't build it". Eight words, and it's the reason the paragraph exists at all.
- **Why "several" happens**, in one clause. Without it, a reader may think it's an odd corner; the point is that it is *guaranteed at every cycle opening*, which is the moment the flag would most want to help.

**Two things I dropped**, per your thinning:

- The `28bd6daa` measurement. The record holds it, and the message's opening already says the record has the measurements.
- The shell-prompt evidence and the "prints what it inferred" forward path. The first is the same point twice; the second is speculation about a design nobody has.

**And I fixed a gap in the record, not just the message.** chores-07 argued only the "several" case — I had never noticed the "none" case, and it's the more common one. It now leads with both, credited to you: `@-` has no bookmark at all through a sub-cycle ladder, where rungs are `jj new` plus `jj describe` and nothing is ever pushed. That makes the argument categorical rather than a list of awkward cases, which is why your two lines beat my eleven.

Draft is 147 lines. Still undelivered, and the chores-07 link placeholder is still open.

Parallel, with one gate. Three reasons, and the third is the one that changed my mind.

**1. The gate: push the opening rung before sending.** The message's first paragraph points at `chores-07.md` and MESSAGES.md says messages are thin pointers, not state. **2. Sequencing costs instances of the exact bug we're reporting.** The duplication item "compounds with every commit either repo writes" — that's the message's own framing. Every commit made while we hold the message is another chance for the two files to drift further apart. Holding a time-sensitive finding to satisfy our own ladder shape is the tail wagging the dog.

**3. The order is actually *better* parallel, not merely faster.** Our rung 2 is the formal review of their agent-file set. If they accept the duplication proposal, `cycle-checklists.md` and `cycle-protocol.md` get restructured — and a review written against today's text is reviewing text that is about to stop existing. So their verdict wants to arrive *before* our review, which means sending now and reviewing after. Sequencing would have us do the review first and throw part of it away.

**Parallel writes are safe by construction.** "Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo. A repo with a live session is written only by its own agent." So three of us on two repos cannot collide on the write side. The only exposure is stale *reads*, and it is confined to the two files under proposal — `prose.md`, `notes.md`, `jj.md`, `versioning.md` and `code.md` are unaffected by the duplication verdict, so the review proceeds on those and brackets the two.

content.text:
Thoughts on the channel, then the push.

**The protocol already answers most of this, and we haven't been following it.** MESSAGES.md says messages are *thin pointers, not state* — "action needed, see `<file>`" rather than restating the details. If a mailbox entry were genuinely three lines pointing at `chores-07.md`, its durability would barely matter: the substance would already be committed in our repo, and losing the pointer would cost a re-send. Our draft is 147 lines. So the durability pain is partly self-inflicted, and it is the same over-writing you caught in chores-07 an hour ago, showing up one layer out.

**The existing mechanism is one commit away from the property it claims.** MESSAGES.md says handled entries may be deleted because "jj history is the archive." vc-x1 measured that the archive does not exist — the template repo is a single `Initial commit` and everything else is uncommitted working copy. Committing it makes the existing sentence true. That is the smallest possible fix, and the reason it hasn't happened is ownership, not design: vc-x1's words were "We are not committing this repo, it not being ours to commit." **A new `vc-x1-messages` repo inherits that exact question** — who commits it, and when — so unless ownership is settled first, we'd rebuild the same failure with a new name.

**Three distinct defects, and the options fix different ones:**

| | durable | notification | threading / lifecycle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mailboxes today | no | no | no |
| mailboxes, committed | yes | no | no |
| `vc-x1-messages` repo | yes | no | weak (commits) |
| GitHub issues | yes | yes | yes |

Notification is the one nobody has named yet and may be the real pain: nothing tells a member mail arrived. We check at acquaint, which is why their 16:47 reply sat unread while three cycles ran past it.

**The cost of issues is not mine to soften — it is vc-x1's own argument, verbatim.** Asking us about trackers for notes entries, they wrote that issues and a database both sit "outside the diff, outside jj history, outside a clone, and off the template payload." Every word applies to messages. Add: a sandboxed agent needs network and auth to read them, offline work stops, and "whose repo hosts them" is a live question, since cross-member mail in one member's issue tracker makes that member the landlord.

**My recommendation.** Keep mailboxes as the pointer channel and make them thin for real — that is the change with the best ratio, and it is free. Fix durability by committing whatever repo hosts them, after settling ownership, because that blocker outlives any choice of mechanism. Hold issues in reserve for when notification proves to be the binding constraint, and if we adopt them, for *proposals* specifically rather than all traffic, since a proposal is the thing that genuinely wants a lifecycle and a thread.

**And these two questions are one question.** vc-x1 asked us whether a notes entry should stay a list item, become a heading, or leave the repo for a tracker, and said our view would be worth more before they pick. This is the same question about a different artifact. Answering them separately risks the family holding two incompatible doctrines about what may live outside the repo. I'd fold this into the formal reply as one position rather than sending it as its own message.

The template repo is already on GitHub as `winksaville/vc-x1-template` — neutral ground, owned by no member. So issues have an obvious host.

**Where I was muddy: I ran three artifacts together.** They have different needs and probably different homes.

1. **The substance** — a finding, a measurement, a proposal. Already durable: it lives in the sender's own chores file, committed and pushed. `chores-07.md` is holding ours right now. Nothing needs to change here.
2. **The notification** — "you have mail." Ephemeral by nature. Losing it costs a re-send, nothing more.
3. **The exchange** — the ask, the verdict, the reasoning behind the verdict, and the fact that it's settled. **This is the homeless one**, and it is what your question is really about.

**The table was answering the wrong question.** It scored durability, notification and threading against the *whole* message, but the substance doesn't need any of the three — it's already in a repo. Only the exchange does. And once you ask only about the exchange, issues stop being a marginal win and become the obvious fit: a thread is exactly ask-plus-answer-plus-resolution, authored by whoever wrote each part, with "closed" meaning handled instead of deleted.

**The gap is specifically the inbound half.** Our findings survive in our chores. vc-x1's verdict and reasoning arrive in a message we are then told to delete, and our only protection is a hand-copy rule — which exists solely to compensate for a transport that loses things, and which already nearly failed once, on the 2026-08-05 convergence measurements.

**So my answer: the exchange lives in an issue; the consequence lives in chores.** Each member records what they *decided* as a result, in their own repo; the argument that got them there lives once, in the thread both parties can write to. The mailbox then has nothing left to carry except notification, and issues already do that.

**On the doctrine objection, head-on.** "Durable context lives in committed files" is a real rule and I don't want to wave it away. But note what it survives on: nothing a member needs in order to *act* would leave the repo. The decision, the rule change, the measurement all still land in chores and travel in a clone. What moves out is the conversation that produced them, with a link from the chores section to the thread. A clone is never missing something it needs; it is missing only the argument, and today the argument is being deleted outright.

**One practical blocker to check before committing to this.** `vc-x1-template`'s remote is `git@github.com:...` — ssh. Our own AGENTS.md bars ssh remotes unconditionally, and a sandboxed agent cannot use one: no auth key readable, and we think a host allowlist cannot admit port 22 at all. For *issues* specifically that may not bite, since `gh` uses the HTTPS API and a token, but any plan that also involves committing that repo hits it immediately. Worth converting the remote regardless.

**And it stays a family decision, not ours.** vc-x1 asked us the identical question about notes entries — list item, heading, or tracker — and asked for our view before they pick. If we answer "tracker" for messages and they answer "stay in the repo" for notes, the family holds two doctrines about what may live outside a clone. I'd put this position in the formal reply as one answer covering both artifacts.

The plain version: substance stays in chores where it already is, the exchange moves to issues on the template repo, and the mailbox shrinks to a notification we may not need. But it goes to vc-x1 as a proposal alongside their own tracker question, not as something we adopt on our own.

**The dual model can't host shared correspondence.** Its ownership rule is "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent" — that rule is *why* mailboxes exist at all. Give the messages repo a manager and it inherits that rule, so members can no longer write to it directly. To leave word you'd have to leave word with the manager, which needs a channel, which is the thing you were building. A manager makes the repo exclusive at exactly the point it needs to be shared.

**And a manager wouldn't fix what actually broke.** `vc-x1-template` is a mess not because nobody supervises it but because **writing and committing were separated** — mail gets dropped in and committing is somebody else's someday. An agent that only runs when invoked isn't an owner, it's one more thing to remember. So the fix is a protocol rule, not a role: **whoever writes an entry commits it in the same act.** Ownership becomes per-write rather than per-repo, and there is no moment at which uncommitted mail exists. A PoR supports that; a managed repo actively obstructs it.

A messages repo gives that beat a commit, and therefore something a trailer can hang from, linking the entry to the session that reasoned it out. That would close a finding rather than just relocating a problem. Caveat: `ochid:` trailers are stamped by `vc-x1 push` across a work/bot *pair*, and hard rule 5 bars hand-writing them, so a third repo would need tooling support. Worth putting in the proposal as a want, not assuming it comes free.

**What it retires.** `custom-family.md`'s "copy anything worth keeping into chores *before* deleting the entry" exists solely because the transport loses things. With durable storage, "handle then delete" becomes "handle then archive", and that rule can go. It nearly failed once already, on the 2026-08-05 convergence measurements.

Two artifacts, two answers, and one of them is honestly unsolved.

**First, a shape change that matters more than the location.** The mailbox-per-*recipient* shape is what creates the problems we keep patching. A mailbox is addressed to a person and drained, so an exchange ends up split across two mailboxes and two repos, each party holding half — which is exactly why the copy-into-chores-before-deleting rule had to exist. If we're building durable storage anyway, **the unit should be the topic, not the recipient**: one file per thread, both parties append, and the conversation is whole in one place.

**So: messages live in `vc-x1-messages` as thread files, with state encoded in location.**

```
vc-x1-messages/
  open/2026-08-13-duplicated-cycle-rules.md
  open/2026-08-13-push-extension.md
  closed/2026-08-05-convergence-positions.md
```

- Anyone appends; whoever resolves it moves the file to `closed/`.
- `ls open/` is the family's open traffic at a glance — the property MESSAGES.md explicitly values, preserved with **no index to maintain**. Moving the file *is* the state change, so nothing is restated and nothing can drift. That's the same rule we've been applying to everything else today.
- Per-thread files make concurrent writes rarer than per-recipient ones did, since two members writing about different topics never touch the same file.

**Why not your own repo**, though it has one genuinely strong argument: a message written into your own repo is a commit `vc-x1 push` already stamps, so the `ochid:` anchor comes free with no tooling change — the third-repo version needs vc-x1 support for that. But it fails on the thing we're trying to fix. Discovery means checking N member repos instead of one place, and an exchange is still split in half, which is the original disease. The substance already lives in your repo and stays there; it's the *exchange* that needs somewhere shared.

**Why not Issues, for this piece**: your own reason, plus mine from last turn. Outside the clone, outside the diff, unreadable offline, and it needs auth from a sandbox. Given you've chosen a PoR, files are the consistent answer.

**Notifications: no good in-repo answer, and I'd rather say so than invent one.** No file in any repo can reach someone who isn't looking. Options are all bad in different ways — polling at acquaint is what we do today and it let vc-x1's 16:47 reply sit unread through three cycles. This is the one artifact Issues genuinely win, because GitHub does the pushing. So my suggestion is: **accept the gap for now**, keep `ls open/` as the acquaint check, and if notification becomes the binding pain, adopt Issues *for notification only* — an issue that carries a link to the thread file and nothing else. That keeps the content in the clone and buys the ping, rather than moving the correspondence out to get it.

**Worth flagging about the scope of this proposal.** Thread-per-topic rewrites MESSAGES.md rather than amending it: mailboxes go, "the recipient deletes" becomes "whoever resolves it closes", and the copy-out rule retires. That's a bigger ask of the family than "new repo, same protocol", and it should go to vc-x1 as such — with the honest note that it comes from us having felt every one of those failure modes in two days.

The plain version: thread files per topic in `vc-x1-messages`, `open/` and `closed/` directories so the filesystem carries the state, and notification stays unsolved on purpose with Issues held in reserve for that one job.

Your instinct is right that we need to answer "what do I owe?" without reading every thread. But I want to push on the mechanism, because `/notifications/<member>.md` is not a notification — it's an **index**, and it's derived state.

**Two problems with it.** First, it doesn't wake anyone: a file in a repo you have to fetch is still polling, just polling a shorter file. Nothing about it reaches a member who isn't already looking. Second, it restates what the threads already know — which member owes what — so it's a second home for a fact, and it will drift the first time someone closes a thread and forgets the index. That is the disease we've spent the whole day naming.

**The version that survives our own rules: put the state in the thread, and make the index a query.** Give each thread a header field:

```
open/2026-08-13-push-extension.md
  Participants: iiac-perf, vc-x1
  Opened: 2026-08-13
  Waiting on: vc-x1
```

Then "what do I owe?" is `grep -l "Waiting on:.*iiac-perf" open/*.md` — exact, zero maintenance, and it cannot go stale because the only place the fact is written is the thread whose state it describes. Whoever replies updates the one line in the file they were already editing. `ls open/` still gives the family view; the grep gives the personal one.

**What real notification would actually take**, so we're choosing with open eyes: something that pushes. GitHub issue mentions into email is the realistic one, which is why I'd hold Issues in reserve for the ping alone — an issue whose body is a link to the thread file and nothing else. Short of that, the honest answer is ergonomic polling: a `vc-x1 messages` subcommand that fetches the repo and runs that grep, made part of acquaint. Same polling we do now, one command instead of a habit, and it fails loudly when the repo is unreachable rather than silently when someone forgets.

**On shared commit rights — you're right that it's a first, and it needs three rules to be boring:**

- **Fetch before you write.** Races are otherwise guaranteed the first time two of us reply in the same hour.
- **Append within a thread, never rewrite another member's entry.** Makes every concurrent write a trivially resolvable merge, and keeps authorship honest.
- **Commit what you write, when you write it.** This is the rule that replaces the manager, and it is the one whose absence turned `vc-x1-template` into a mess.

And say explicitly in the protocol that **this repo is the deliberate exception** to "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent." That rule assumes an agent owns the repo; a PoR has none, which is exactly what makes shared commit safe here. Leaving it unsaid invites a future session to refuse to write on principle.

**Two setup details worth getting right at birth:** create it with an **https** remote, not ssh, or a sandboxed agent cannot push to it — `vc-x1-template` has `git@github.com:` today and that is a live trap. And no `.claude`, since PoR was the decision.

The plain version: drop `/notifications/`, put `Waiting on:` in each thread header and let grep be the inbox, and accept that nothing in a repo can truly notify — with Issues held in reserve for that one job if polling keeps failing us.
