My thread-files design needed new vc-x1 tooling to get that; yours gets it for free, and it closes this morning's "beats with no work-repo commit have no anchor" finding rather than relocating it. The dual local+remote reference is also better than either of my options: the local path works with a sibling clone, the URL works without one.

**One thing will break, and it will break on our very first message.** The remote reference has to be a **commit-SHA permalink**, not a branch path. Two reasons:

- The example URL is malformed — `https://github.com/iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1` has no owner and no `blob/<ref>`. The real shape is `https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/<ref>/messages/test-msg.md#message1`.
- More seriously: if `<ref>` is a topic bookmark, **the link dies when the bookmark is deleted at close-out**, which hard rule 13 requires. Our pending message points into `chores-07.md` on `docs-converge-the-agent-files-with-vc-x1`, and that bookmark is scheduled for deletion. A `main` ref is no better, since the message is written before landing and `main` doesn't have the file yet.

A SHA permalink is the only form valid at both ends, and the family already does this — chores as-built rungs store `/commit/<12-hex>` for exactly this reason. GitHub's `y` key produces it.

**Cheap tightenings, none structural:**

- **Pin "somewhere in your repo."** Your example implies `<repo>/messages/*.md`. Say so, or four members invent four conventions and finding an old message becomes archaeology.
- **Say the entry is deleted when handled.** Otherwise the file is an append-only log with no signal, and "what's unread" stops being answerable. This is now *safe* to do, which it never was before: with the body in the sender's repo, deleting a notification line loses nothing. That single property is what retires `custom-family.md`'s copy-out rule.
- **Timestamp in UTC with the `Z`**, matching your own shell prompt (`26-08-13T16:17:59.041Z`). Costs one character, removes a whole class of ambiguity.
- **Name the sender in the line.** It's currently inferable from the path only if the path convention holds, and one word makes `grep` by sender work.
- **Note that local refs assume sibling clones**, since `../iiac-perf-test1/...` is relative to the messages repo.

**One open question worth settling now:** does this README supersede `MESSAGES.md`, or does `MESSAGES.md` become a pointer to it? Two protocol documents is the nine-steps problem in miniature, and we're about to send vc-x1 a message complaining about exactly that.

**And it's additive-friendly**, which is why I'd stop here as you say. Nothing in this design blocks adding threads, or `open/`/`closed/`, or issue-based pings later — notifications are orthogonal to whatever holds the exchange. Simple first is the right call, and the loss to accept meanwhile is that a conversation lives as a chain of cross-repo links rather than one object. Cheapest hedge: when you write a reply, have its section link back to the section it answers, so the chain is walkable in both directions for free.

The plain version: the design is sound and better than mine on the anchor question; make the remote reference a commit-SHA permalink or our first message will rot, and add three lines saying where message files live, that entries are deleted when handled, and that timestamps are UTC.

content.text:
Persistence is the better call, and for a reason stronger than "could": **it collapses the write surface to senders only.**

With delete-when-handled, every member writes to the shared repo *twice* per exchange — once to send, once to record "I read it" — and that second write is a fetch, edit, commit and push carrying zero information. With persistence, readers only read. Only senders ever write, which makes the shared-commit-rights question much smaller than it looked two turns ago: collisions can only happen between two senders writing to the same recipient's file at the same moment.

The copy-out rule still retires, by a more direct route than I gave: there's no deletion to guard against at all.

**The consequence to accept: "unread" becomes reader-side.** The file no longer tells you what you've handled. In practice that's fine — newest at top, UTC timestamps, read down until you reach one you recognize — and what you handled is recorded in your own chores anyway, so the answer already exists on your side. Worth stating the bias explicitly in the README: **re-reading a handled entry is harmless, missing one is not**, so read one too far rather than one too few.

**On the URL, one distinction to be sure of: "full" isn't the same as "permanent."** The ref has to be a commit SHA. `blob/main/...` is well-formed and still wrong for us today — the file isn't on `main` yet — and `blob/<bookmark>/...` dies when hard rule 13 deletes the bookmark at close-out.

Concretely, for the message waiting to go out. The opening pushed as `a69f2d45d3d2`, so its permanent form is:

```
https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#message-to-vc-x1-duplicated-cycle-rules-and-landing
```

That survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything after it, and resolves for someone with no clone. The `#`-anchor is the slug our own algorithm produces and the anchor checker has already validated it.

The plain version: persist, because it means readers never have to write; the price is that "have I handled this?" is answered from your own records, and the fix is to re-read rather than risk skipping.

# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo; this repo holds
only pointers to them, one line per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then insert a single line notification at the top of a file based on the destination's name
you find here. That single line is of the form:

    utc-date-timestamp: local-file-reference, remote-file-reference

Where the file reference has an optional markdown section slug, example:

    2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1, https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

When a message has been read add "read" after the utc-date-timestamp 

    2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: read ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1, https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A line with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day; anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Entries persist

Nothing here is deleted. A notification is a permanent line in a log, newest at the top.

- **Readers never write.** Marking an entry handled would mean a fetch, an edit, a commit and a
  push carrying no information, so the only writer of a member's file is whoever sends to that
  member.
- **So this repo cannot tell you what you have already handled.** Read from the top down until
  you reach an entry you recognize; what you handled is recorded in your own repo anyway.
- **Re-reading a handled entry is harmless and missing one is not**, so read one too far rather
  than one too few.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  line can be lost without losing anything.

**On read-marking: `read` over deletion, and I'm reversing my own argument from two turns ago.**

I said readers should never write, because marking costs a fetch-edit-commit-push "carrying no information." That was wrong, and the thing I missed is **who the receipt is for**. Whether a message was read is recorded nowhere else — not in your repo, not in mine. Without the marker the sender never learns their message landed, and "did they see it yet?" becomes another thing to ask about. That is real information, and it earns the small commit. Deletion would carry the same cost while also destroying the log you wanted persisted, so it loses on both counts.

The README's persistence section said the opposite, so I've rewritten it: the receipt is for the sender, unread is the absence of the marker, and no separate state exists anywhere.

**One refinement worth considering, not applied since you'd already chosen the format:** `read` could carry its own timestamp, either in place or appended — `2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: read@2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z ...`. It answers "how long did that sit?", which is the question that actually bit us yesterday when vc-x1's reply waited three cycles. Bare `read` answers only "eventually". Your call — the bare token is simpler and simple was the brief.

**On optional links, added as two bullets.** The rule is at least one, never neither. And the asymmetry is worth a reader knowing: **the local form names a path, the remote names a version.** A local reference resolves to whatever that file says *now*, in whatever state that working copy happens to be — so if the sender edits the message file afterwards, a local-only link silently shows the new text, not what was sent. Local-only is fine for same-day traffic; anything meant to be read later wants the remote.

That's also why I'd resist making remote optional *in practice* even though it's optional *in the format*: our own message to vc-x1 is exactly the case that gets read after the bookmark is gone.

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled entry. A sender needs to know none of that, only

control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

content.text:
Good idea, and for a bigger reason than convenience: **it turns each line into a complete exchange.**

Right now a receipt says "seen" and stops. The sender then has to hunt for what came of it. With the payload, one line carries the message *and* its disposition — which quietly recovers the property we gave up when we dropped thread files. I argued then that a conversation would become "a chain of cross-repo links rather than one object", and suggested replies link back manually. This mechanizes that, and it costs one optional field instead of a directory structure and a state machine.

**Three things I'd pin down before it goes in:**

**1. Name what goes in it.** "Relevant info" is vague, and vague fields fill with whatever the writer felt like that day. I'd say the links point at *what came of the message* — the reply, or the record of the decision. Then the field has one meaning and a reader knows what they're getting.

**2. State that both forms are valid, and that they mean different things.** Bare `read` is "I saw it." `read:[...]` is "I saw it, and here is what came of it." That degrades cleanly: you mark `read` when you've looked, and you can only fill the payload once you've acted, which are genuinely different moments. Worth saying out loud, or someone will treat a bare `read` as an incomplete `read:[...]` and feel obliged to backfill it.

**3. Your placement is right, and I nearly argued otherwise.** I was going to say push it to the end so the message reference stays scannable — but the timestamp is fixed-width, so `read` always lands at the same column. That makes the unread scan trivially visual, and the bracket payload sits after the token without disturbing it. Keep it where you have it.

**The one real cost is line length.** A fully populated line has four references:

```
2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: read:[../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push, https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push] ../vc-x1/messages/msg.md#m1, https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/076193f9/messages/msg.md#m1
```

Which is unreadable in a terminal without wrap. Two mitigations, neither urgent: the optional-links rule already lets you drop the local form when the remote exists, roughly halving it; and nothing stops a reader from using only the local link in their receipt, since the receipt points into their own repo and they always have it. So in practice most lines will carry two references, not four.

**Syntax is parseable**, which matters if `vc-x1 messages` ever wants to read these. The brackets nest unambiguously, so a parser splits on the first `:`, checks for a `read` token, matches the bracket pair, then splits the remainder on comma. Not trivially splittable on comma alone, but never ambiguous — which is the property that actually matters.

The plain version: yes, add it, because it makes one line hold both halves of an exchange. Call the payload "what came of it" rather than "relevant info", say that bare `read` and `read:[...]` both mean something, and keep it right after the timestamp where the fixed-width column makes it scannable.

content.text:
Your instinct is right, and the evidence is this conversation: the one-line format has been revised **four times in about an hour** — the base line, then `read`, then optional references, then the `read:[...]` payload. A grammar that keeps changing is telling you it wants to be a container with named fields rather than positions.

**Two shapes fit "one or more lines with a separator", and they're not the same decision.**

**A: a markdown record per header.**

```markdown
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- msg: ../vc-x1/messages/msg.md#m1
- url: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/076193f9/messages/msg.md#m1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
```

**B: the markdown-carried TOML format**, one fence per record, fields typed and validated by the same `md_fence.rs` path vc-x1 already ships.

**The property that tips it for me is anchors.** A `##` header per record gives every notification a *slug*, so a reply can link at the exact entry it answers, and a chores section can cite the notification it acted on. Cross-linking stops needing invented IDs, because the timestamp is already unique. A TOML fence has no anchor unless you put a heading above it anyway — at which point you have both shapes and the fence is buying only types.

**What B buys that A doesn't:** a machine-checkable schema and a parser that already exists. That matters exactly if something will parse these — the `vc-x1 messages` command I floated for acquaint-time polling. If that gets built, typed records beat scraping list items.

**What B costs, and this is the part I'd weigh hardest:** it couples the family's messaging protocol to a capability that is itself mid-flight. `.vc-config.md` is on vc-x1's current cycle, the `toml`-tag escape is documented only in our message to them, and the `config --toml` debugger we asked for is ranked but unbuilt. If the fence rules move, our message store moves with them. Also the live-fence trap bites here in a new way: a message *about* TOML, quoting a config, would silently become a record unless escaped.

**So my lean: A now, B later if a tool needs it.** The migration runs cleanly in that direction — named list items map to TOML keys mechanically — and A needs no dependency, no escape rule, and gets anchors today. Going the other way, from typed records back to prose, is the lossy direction.

**One caution, offered because you're the one who said "real simple."** We are three format revisions past that, in a conversation whose subject is that we over-write things. Whatever we pick should be the last pick for a while, and that is actually the strongest argument for your proposal: a record with named fields absorbs the next four changes without a redesign, where the line needed one each time. Pick the container, then stop designing the container.

The plain version: yes to multi-line records with a separator, use markdown headers rather than TOML fences for now, take the free anchors, and switch to TOML only if something is actually going to parse them.

# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo; this repo holds
only pointers to them, one line per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then insert a single line notification at the top of a file based on the destination's name
you find here. That single line is of the form:

    utc-date-timestamp: local-file-reference, remote-file-reference

Where the file reference has an optional markdown section slug, example:

    2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1, https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

When a message has been read add "read" after the utc-date-timestamp 

    2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z: read ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1, https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A line with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day; anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled entry. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add a line.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled entry tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes the line tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  line can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo; this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
```

- **The heading is a UTC timestamp and the sender.** It is also the record's anchor, so a reply
  or a record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.
- **`local` and `remote`** are the message's file references, each with an optional markdown
  section slug.
- **`read`** is added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it
  is unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
- **`outcome-local` / `outcome-remote`** are optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what
  came of the message: the reply, or the record of what was decided. They are what let one entry
  hold both halves of an exchange.

A handled record with all of them:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
```

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record; only the field lines are read.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A line with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day; anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled entry. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add a line.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled entry tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes the line tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  line can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

Format A is in, with the fields named for the vocabulary the README already used.

**The record:**

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local:  ../vc-x1/messages/msg.md#m1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/blob/076193f9/messages/msg.md#m1
- read:   2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local:  ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/…
```

**Four things the shape settled that the line format kept re-opening:**

- **The heading carries the sender**, which I'd suggested twice and dropped both times because it didn't fit a positional line. Here it's free.
- **The heading is the anchor**, so a reply or a chores section can link at one exact record with no invented id — the reason A beat the TOML fences.
- **`read` is a timestamp, not a token**, so "how long did it sit?" is answerable. That was the refinement I raised on the bare marker and you'd have had to choose against; with named fields there's no cost to it.
- **Unread is the absence of a field**, so open traffic is still derived, nothing tracked twice.

Plus the stated escape hatch: fields may be added later, unknown fields are ignored, a record missing an optional field is complete — which is the whole reason you wanted records, so it's written down rather than implied.

**Swept three leftovers from the line era** that would otherwise have read as a second format: "one line per message" in the intro, "a line with neither" in the permalink rules, and "where to add a line" in the persistence section.

**And updated `iiac-perf.md`'s policy** to match: records never deleted, handled ones gain a `read` timestamp, and where it led lives in that same record's `outcome-*` fields rather than in prose pointing at chores. That's tighter than what I wrote an hour ago — the record now carries its own disposition instead of telling you where to go look.

Both files still uncommitted in `@`.

Noted — I'll stop reaching for them.

One thing worth surfacing rather than just absorbing, because it explains why I keep doing it. `prose.md`'s rule permits the antithesis case: "A semicolon earns its place only between equals: two parallel claims of the same weight, where the contrast is the point," with the worked example `The diff empties; the history keeps the record`. All four I wrote were that shape — bodies there / pointers here, same-day / later, protocol there / policy here. So I wasn't ignoring the rule, I was reading it as a licence, and I'll keep landing in the same place until the written rule and your preference agree.

If your actual line is "no semicolons in this family's prose," that's a one-word change to `prose.md` and it saves us both this friction. And it's the same finding we've been collecting all day: a rule that says one thing while practice says another, which is worth a bullet in the message to vc-x1 if you want it.

Separately, and not a style matter: your edit to `iiac-perf.md` left the second half as `` - `` with a leading space, which markdown renders as a one-item bullet list hanging off the paragraph. Since that file is mine to curate under the ownership rule, I made it two sentences instead — no semicolon, no stray list.

Everything in that repo is still uncommitted in `@`.

always believes the two halves are equals, so the carve-out was claimed by every use and the rule
permitted what it was written to bar. A flat ban needs no judgment call and costs a full stop.

[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws. A semicolon inside a code span is
syntax, and one inside quoted or transcribed text is data. Neither is prose, and neither is swept.

- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72

solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
terminals, where the markers survive; if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
is wrong to normalize them.
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.

The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
because a commit cannot record its own SHA; a Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
records, while the rule outlives it.

**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file; leave the evidence trail
in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
14	or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
15	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
16	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
17	fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
18	they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
19	naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
20	[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
21	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
28	  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
32	  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
33	  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
34	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).
35	
36	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
37	
38	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged
39	  by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
40	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
41	    meets first and it answers the problem
42	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
43	    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
44	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
45	    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
46	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
47	    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
48	    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
49	    here
50	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
51	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
52	  list. See
53	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
54	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
55	
56	### Line widths
57	
58	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
59	than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
60	2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
61	
62	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
63	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
64	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
65	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
66	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
67	  convention here 2026-08-09. Published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
68	
69	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
70	when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
71	imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
72	a literal report row, indented code in a comment).
73	
74	### Problem-first shape
75	
76	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
77	form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
78	
79	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
80	  what follows it.
81	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
82	  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in

`prose.md` updated and now obeys its own rule.

**The rule.** "Durable prose authors none." The antithesis case joins the other two as something to fix rather than a licence — two sentences, or a comma with a conjunction. The authoring-not-presence carve-out stays, matching the typeable-punctuation rule: a semicolon in a code span is syntax, one in quoted or transcribed text is data, neither gets swept. The one remaining semicolon in the file is line 134, the quoted example of what not to write, which is naming the character rather than using it.

**I recorded why the exception went**, since the family has to evaluate this: a writer reaching for a semicolon always believes the two halves are equals, so the carve-out was claimed by every use and the rule permitted what it was written to bar. My four this evening were all self-classified that way, which is the evidence.

**And I swept prose.md's own six**, because a rule file that breaks its own rule is the weakest possible thing to send vc-x1.

**The cost of adopting it, measured**, since you'll want it before proposing:

- **~45 lines** across `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/*` contain a semicolon outside an inline code span. That's an upper bound — the sample shows some are inside fenced Rust examples in `code.md`, which are syntax. A precise number needs the authored-versus-transcribed judgment the rule itself calls for, which is why a byte scan isn't the rule.
- **34 lines in `custom-family.md`**, ours alone and not part of any family proposal.
- **This is the second sweep in six days.** vc-x1's 2026-08-08 message reports converting ~140 joins set-wide under the rule we're now replacing. Asking them to re-sweep files they just swept is the honest headline of the proposal, and leaving it out would be the kind of omission we'd notice if it came the other way.

**One open question: which rung carries this.** "Convention work runs as its own cycle" bars inserting a convention itch into a feature ladder, but this cycle's whole subject is agent-file convergence, so the rule change is on-topic rather than an intrusion. I'd hang it on rung 2 with the review, and let the set-wide sweep be its own cycle after vc-x1 rules on it — sweeping ~45 lines now would bury the review under mechanical churn.

Nothing swept beyond `prose.md`, and none of it committed.

content.text:
Agree with expunging. I'd argue against it being *in* rung 2, and the strongest reason is vc-x1's own words.

**Their 2026-08-08 message, on their own semicolon sweep:** "The semicolon sweep converted ~140 joins set-wide, so your diff against us shows one rule applied many times; review the rule, not each instance." They had to tell us to skip the instances. Rung 2's entire job is making our differences reviewable — the formal review, the verdicts, the 0.24.8 proposal. # vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
```

### **The heading is a UTC timestamp and the sender.**
  It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone 
  inventing an id. This is followed by a dash list of  `- field: <value>` and references
  may have an option section slug. The - `outcome-local` / `outcome-remote` are optional, added by the
  recipient, pointing at what came of the message: the reply, or the record of what was decided. They are
  what let one entry hold both halves of an exchange.

- `local:` a message's local file reference
- `remote:` a message's remote file reference
- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it
  is unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
- `outcome-local:` a message's outcome-local file reference 
- `outcome-remote:` a message's outcome-iremote file reference


A handled record with all of them:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
```

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A record with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

**1. We cannot send to vc-x1, and the protocol doesn't say how to fix it.** The repo holds `README.md` and `iiac-perf.md`. There is no `vc-x1.md`. "Each file's owner sets its persistence" says the owner creates their own file — so a sender facing a member who hasn't created theirs has no legal move, and we hit this the moment we deliver the message we've been drafting all evening. Needs one sentence: either a sender may create the file with a default policy, or every member creates theirs at join time and the family seeds them now.

**2. The commit rule is missing entirely.** "You commit what you write, when you write it" is the rule that replaces the manager and prevents the exact failure that made `vc-x1-template` unusable. It's the single most important operational rule here and it appears nowhere in the README. Everything else in the file is format; this is the one that decides whether the repo works.

**3. The two examples disagree, and it changes the anchor.** Line 12 is `## …123Z from vc-x1`, line 36 is `## …123Z vc-x1`. Since the heading *is* the record's anchor, those slug differently — `#2026-08-13t193121123z-from-vc-x1` versus `#…z-vc-x1` — so a cross-link written against one form breaks against the other. And the heading's format is only ever shown, never stated as a rule.

**4. Three text bugs:** line 21 reads "The - `outcome-local`" with a stray list marker; line 30 says `outcome-iremote`; line 20 says "an option section slug" for "optional".

**5. The `outcome-*` explanation lives in two places.** The substance is in the paragraph at 21-23, while the field list at 29-30 has the thin restatements ("a message's outcome-local file reference"). Same for `local`/`remote`: the list entries are tautologies of their own names. Meanwhile `read:` carries its real explanation in the list. So the list is half substantive and half empty, with the missing half sitting above it — item-plus-detail split across two homes, which is the thing this family reliably regrets.

I'd fold everything into the field list and let the prose above it stop at the heading-is-an-anchor point.

**6. `### **The heading is …**`** is a heading and bold at once, and it sits mid-flow between the example and the field list where it used to be a bullet. Its continuation lines are indented two spaces under a heading, which does nothing. Reads like a bullet that got promoted by accident.

**Two smaller things**, take or leave: "somewhere in your repo" is still unpinned even though both examples use `messages/`, so the convention exists in practice but not in writing. And two records from the same sender in the same millisecond would collide on their anchor and silently resolve to the first — vanishingly unlikely at ms precision, worth a clause only if you want the format to be airtight.

**What's good and I'd not touch:** the permalink section is the strongest part and it's the one that will save an actual link from rotting. "No protection" is exactly the right length. And the field-list-over-positional-line reasoning at 45-48 states *why* the format is what it is, which is what will stop the next person re-litigating it.

Want me to apply 1-6?

# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
```

The heading is `<utc-timestamp> from <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.

Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
section slug:

- `local:` the message's local file reference.
- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
  unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
  both halves of an exchange.

A handled record with all of them:

```
## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z from vc-x1

- local: ../iiac-perf-test1/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf-test1/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push
```

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read.

## Write and commit in one act

Whoever writes a record commits it, in the same act. There is then no moment at which an
uncommitted record exists, and nobody has to remember to commit someone else's writing later.
This repo has no manager and needs none, because ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A record with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

content.text:
Yes, with one real gap and two I'd flag but wouldn't block on.

**The gap worth closing before they see it: who may edit which fields.** It is the one place two members write the same lines. The sender creates a record and owns `local`/`remote`. The recipient later adds `read` and the `outcome-*` fields *into that same record*. Nothing says that's the division, or that neither party rewrites the other's fields. Right now a reader could reasonably conclude the recipient may tidy a sender's reference, or that a sender may correct their own record after it's been read. In a repo with no access control, the only thing preventing that is a sentence, and there isn't one.

**Two I'd flag but leave:**

- **"Somewhere in your repo"** is still unpinned though both examples use `messages/`. Four members inventing four conventions costs you the day you go hunting an old message. One clause fixes it, and I've raised it three times now, so if it's deliberate say so and I'll stop.
- **A reply doesn't link back to the record it answers.** `outcome-*` gets you forward from a message to its result, but nothing gets you from a reply back to what prompted it. One convention — a reply's record cites the anchor it answers — makes an exchange walkable in both directions, which was the property we gave up when we chose notification records over thread files.

**One I'd explicitly *not* add:** fetch-before-you-write. I listed it earlier as a needed rule and I now think it isn't, because `jj git push` refuses a non-fast-forward and says so. It fails loudly, so the README doesn't need to teach it.

**And one thing I'd leave deliberately unspecified**, in case it looks like an omission when vc-x1 reads it: the shape of the message file in the sender's repo. One file per message, or a file that accumulates sections, is the sender's business, and the only contract is that the reference resolves. That's correct as-is, and might be worth one sentence saying it's intentional rather than forgotten.

So: yes, I'm content with it. It states its rules with reasons, which is the thing that lets them argue with it properly. I'd add the who-edits-what sentence, and I'd be happy for the rest to go to them as-is — the two open questions I'd rather they answer than we guess.

content.text:
It closes the gap, and "owned by the creator" is the better form of what I asked for — a principle that derives the division (sender owns `local`/`remote`, recipient owns `read` and `outcome-*`) instead of enumerating it. Three things I'd change.

**1. Placement, and there's a visible symptom.** The sentence used to end "…a list of fields:" with the colon introducing the example. Now it ends on ownership, so the code block that follows illustrates a sentence about who may edit what. The block is showing you a *record*, and the prose immediately above it is about permissions. Ownership is a rule about editing, not part of the definition of a record, and it arrives before the reader knows what the fields even are.

I'd put it right after the field list, where the reader can map it onto `local`/`remote` versus `read`/`outcome-*`.

**2. The hedges undo the rule.** "Generally" and "although fixing errors is permissible" reintroduce exactly the ambiguity the sentence is meant to remove. What counts as an error — a typo in a slug, a `remote` pointing at the wrong commit, a timestamp you believe is off? Under that clause I may edit your record, and now it says something you didn't write.

And the permission is redundant: `## No protection` already says anyone can modify or delete anything and history is the recourse. That section states what is *possible*. This one should state what is *expected*, and it's stronger without the escape hatch.

**3. It's a run-on** with two `and`s doing different work, which the no-semicolon rule pushes toward splitting anyway.

Concrete wording, after the field list:

```
Each field is owned by whoever created it. The sender writes the heading, `local` and `remote`,
the recipient adds `read` and the `outcome-*` fields, and neither rewrites the other's.
```

That keeps your principle, names the instance so nobody has to derive it, and lets `No protection` keep its job.

**One edge I'd leave alone unless you want it**: nothing stops a sender editing their own `local` or `remote` after a `read` receipt exists, which changes what the recipient was recorded as having read. The permalink makes it harmless for `remote`, and this is a friendly-participants system. Mentioning it would cost more than it buys.

Worth separating two problems, because one of them may not exist.

**Real records are not in fences.** In `iiac-perf.md` a record is plain markdown, and GFM autolinks bare `https://` in text. So `remote:` is already clickable in the place where clicking matters. Only `local:` isn't, because relative paths never autolink — no scheme.

That maps onto the distinction the README already draws — local names a path, remote names a version. It renders exactly as a live record does — links live — because it *is* one, and it doubles as the thing someone copies when creating their own file. content.text:
Looked. Four concrete bugs first, then the approach.

**1. The `[1]` and the path both render.** `- local: [1] ../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1` is a shortcut reference link *followed by* literal text, so it renders as:

> local: **1** ../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1

A cryptic clickable "1", and then the same path again as unclickable plain text. That's both costs and neither benefit.

**2. The two example headings are identical**, so they produce duplicate anchors and GitHub silently suffixes the second. In the document whose whole point is that the heading *is* the record's anchor, that's an unfortunate demonstration.

**3. `local` and `remote` name different repos** — `../iiac-perf/messages/...` against `.../iiac-perf-test1/blob/...`. They should be the same repo, since they're two references to one message.

**4. `## References` at the end is empty**, while the actual `[1]:` definition sits at line 41 in the middle of the document.

**On the approach.** Reference-style links solve clickability but cost more than they look. The rendered result is a bare "1" — you can't see where it goes without hovering, which is worse than a plain readable path. And the README is the spec: if it shows `[1]`, every member file will grow a `References` section and a number namespace to maintain. That's the machinery `TODO.md` renumbering already taught us to dislike, and here it would be per-file across the family.

**If `local` must be clickable, the least-bad form is an inline link with short text:**

```
- local: [test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
```

Renders as a readable clickable `test-msg.md#message1`, the full path lives once in the target, no reference section, no numbering, nothing to maintain. Cost is that a parser reading `local:` gets markdown syntax to strip rather than a bare path.

**But I'd still ask whether it must be.** `remote` autolinks for free and is the human-facing, durable, works-without-a-clone one. `local` is the machine-facing form, resolved by an agent walking the filesystem, and it's the one that can silently point at edited content. Leaving it as plain text costs a human one copy-paste and keeps the format free of markdown syntax in its values.

**And dropping the fences has a cost worth weighing separately from clickability**: the examples are now real sections in the README's outline, and a reader skimming the file structure sees two timestamp headings among the rules. The specimen-file idea sidesteps that — `example.md` as a real member file with live records — but it is one more file, and "real simple" is the brief.

**Second cost, smaller but ironic:** the examples are now real `##` sections, both with identical headings, so they collide on anchor in the document that teaches that the heading *is* the anchor.

**The resolution I'd take: fences in the README, and `iiac-perf.md` as the live specimen.** It already exists, it will accumulate real records with real resolvable targets, and it renders. So the spec shows syntax and the member file shows the result — no `example.md`, no extra file, and clickability lands where it's actually useful.

So: leave bare-versus-inline free and see what wears well, and don't model the reference form in the spec. It also renders worst of the three — a cryptic "1" followed by the same path as plain text.

content.text:
The `[[1]]` / `[[2]]` form renders cleanly, but I'd argue against it here for a reason that's structural rather than aesthetic.

**Reference numbers are shared state inside a file that two people write concurrently.** Every record needs the next free number, so two senders adding records to `iiac-perf.md` in the same hour both reach for `[7]`. Merge that and you get two `[7]:` definitions — CommonMark takes the first, so one record silently points at the other's target. A wrong link that renders perfectly. Inline links have no shared namespace and cannot do this.

**And the value has now left the record entirely.** `local: [[1]]` carries no path at all, so a record copied into a chores section, quoted in a message, or pasted anywhere is meaningless. That matters more here than usual, because `outcome-*` exists precisely so records get cited elsewhere. The earlier `[1] path` at least kept the value as text.

**Third, smaller:** a parser reading `local:` must now implement markdown reference resolution rather than strip `[text](target)`.

**Why it works in chores and not here:** there, a rung cites the same commit URL repeatedly and the line must stay short, so indirection pays. Here each reference is cited once, the file is append-only, and the numbers grow forever with nobody re-packing them.

So my suggestion for "leave it undefined": leave the *style* free — bare path and `[path](path)` both fine, let usage decide — but fix one invariant, that **the value appears in the record**. That rules out reference forms without ruling on the two that survive being moved.

**The better finding from your note about them being broken until pushed: the send procedure has an ordering constraint the README doesn't state.** A permalink can only be written after the commit containing the message exists and is pushed — `blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md` 404s today because that file was created after that commit. So sending is really:

1. write the message file in your repo
2. commit and push it
3. *then* add the record, with the SHA that push produced

The README currently says create the file, then add the record, with no hint that step 2 sits between them. Every sender hits this once, and it's one sentence to prevent.

It also interacts with something we already decided: `local` needs no push, so a same-day local-only record can be written immediately, while a record meant to last has to wait for the push. That's the local-versus-remote distinction showing up as a workflow difference rather than just a durability one.

content.text:
Local-only as a mode is right, and it does more than permit an omission — it removes the ordering constraint entirely.

**Two modes fall out, and the README could just say so:**

- **Fast dialog, local only.** Write the message file, write the record, done. No push, no permalink, no waiting. The reader resolves it from their sibling clone. This is the mode where you and I go back and forth in an evening.
- **Durable, with a permalink.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then write the record with the SHA that push produced. The extra step buys a reference that survives the bookmark's deletion and works for a reader with no clone.

That framing also answers the ordering problem from last turn: it only exists in the second mode, and stating the modes states the ordering for free.

**On empty values, I'd push back.** They add a third state — has-value, present-but-empty, absent — where two carry the meaning. And the thing empty would encode is *workflow* ("a permalink is coming"), not data. Records are what the exchange was; the fact that you haven't pushed yet belongs in your own repo, not in the recipient's file.

The honest case for it: a record with only `local` is ambiguous between "deliberately ephemeral" and "the permalink isn't written yet", and the recipient can't tell which. That's a real signal.

But the cheaper fix is the ordering rule: **don't write the record until you have what goes in it.** Writing it twice, once empty and once filled, is two commits to the shared repo for one message — and the reader may see the empty one, follow nothing, and mark it read. Waiting costs the sender a minute and keeps the format at two states.

**One thing that does deserve saying explicitly**, since local-only is now a first-class mode rather than a fallback: a local-only record is unreadable to anyone without the sibling clone, and it resolves to whatever that file says *now* rather than what was sent. Fine for same-day traffic between siblings, wrong for anything you'd want to cite later. The README has both halves of that already, in the permalink section — they just aren't connected to the choice of mode.

costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
permissible.

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1

- local: [../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.

Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
section slug.

- `local:` the message's local file reference.
- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
  unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
  both halves of an exchange.

A handled record with all of them:

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1

- local: [[1]]
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: [[2]]
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push

[1]: ../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1
[2]: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read.

## Two modes, fast and durable

The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.

- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
  that push made resolvable.

**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.

**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
push.

## Write and commit in one act

Whoever writes a record commits it, in the same act. There is then no moment at which an
uncommitted record exists, and nobody has to remember to commit someone else's writing later.
This repo has no manager and needs none, because ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A record with neither points at nothing.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. **This one is
  a proposal rather than a settled rule**, and the first thing worth vc-x1's opinion.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

It contradicts a rule already in the file. Line 11 says all fields are optional. Line 91 says:

> **Either reference may be omitted, but not both.** A record with neither points at nothing.

Both can't be the rule. And the smiley concedes the tension without resolving it — "isn't very useful" is advice, "not both" is a constraint.

**The deeper question underneath, which is worth deciding rather than leaving to interpretation.** Line 48 says prose may sit beside the fields in a record. Combine that with all-fields-optional and a record can carry the message *itself* — heading, no references, body inline. For a one-word reply that's genuinely attractive, and I suspect it's what "quite typical" is reaching toward.

But it breaks the repo's founding invariant. The intro says bodies live in the sender's repo and this holds only pointers, and the persistence section rests on it: "a notification record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe." Let a record hold a body and something *is* only here — so an owner whose declared policy is deletion can now destroy the only copy of a message, and `## No protection` stops being survivable.

**Two coherent positions, and I'd take the first:**

1. **Every field is optional, with one constraint: at least one of `local` or `remote`.** Short traffic still costs a two-line file in your own repo, which is cheap and keeps the invariant absolute.
2. **Records may carry bodies inline**, in which case the intro's "only pointers" claim and the persistence section's safety argument both need rewriting, and owner-chosen deletion policies become dangerous rather than free.

If you take 1, I'd state it once where the fields are defined and drop the bullet at line 91, leaving the permalink section to argue only SHA-versus-branch and path-versus-version. Something like:

```
Every field is optional, with one constraint. A record needs at least one of `local` or
`remote`, since a record with neither points at nothing.
```

Small thing beside that: "it's quite typical" has no referent — typical of what? Presumably that records routinely omit fields, which is worth saying plainly since it tells a reader that a two-field record is normal rather than incomplete.

content.text:
Both stances hold — they're aimed at different actors. **Strict for writers, tolerant for readers.** "A record needs at least one reference" is advice to whoever writes one. "A reader takes what is there rather than rejecting the record" is the tolerance. Line 11 currently reads as a writer permission ("all fields are optional") when what you mean is reader tolerance, which is why it collides with line 91.

**But the failure modes aren't equal, and one of them isn't benign.** Ranked by what they cost:

- **A missing field** — the record is less useful and nothing else suffers. Genuinely no harm.
- **A missing sender**, heading otherwise intact — recoverable, because "write and commit in one act" means whoever wrote the record committed it, so the author is in the history. Worth noting your own scenario is the exception: if someone else commits an interrupted write, that recovery goes with it.
- **A missing timestamp**, sender intact — the heading becomes `## vc-x1`, which still separates records but collides on anchor with every other record from that sender. Citations silently resolve to the first. Ordering survives, since newest-first is positional rather than sorted.
- **A missing `##` heading entirely** — this is the one that isn't benign. The heading is the record separator, so orphaned field lines are read as part of the record *above*. An interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself, and the damage is invisible: the previous record just appears to have extra fields.

So I'd say the tolerant framing is right, with exactly one hard requirement, justified by consequence rather than by fiat:

```
A record missing fields is not an error, only less useful, and a reader takes what is there
rather than rejecting it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading, because it is
what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as
part of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
```

That also resolves line 11 against line 91 without either of them moving much: everything is optional to a reader, a writer aims for at least one reference, and the heading is structural rather than informational.

content.text:
Yes to committing `vc-x1-messages` — its own founding rule is "write and commit in one act", and it has sat uncommitted for hours, which is precisely the `vc-x1-template` failure we're documenting. Two things to settle first:

- **`.claude/` and `.mcp.json` appeared in it.** A plain repo with no agent shouldn't track a session directory, so it wants a `.gitignore` before the first commit rather than after.
- **The example permalinks 404 until `messages/test-msg.md` is committed and pushed here.** Which is the ordering rule we just wrote, applied to us: the record can't carry a permalink until the commit exists. So the sequence is iiac-perf push, then update the README's SHAs, then commit the messages repo. That dogfoods the rule on its first use, which is worth more than the two minutes it costs.

**On saving `prose.md`: jj already has.** The working copy is a real change (`pnowzzty…`) and `jj op log` retains it, so the edits aren't at risk the way uncommitted git work is. Saving isn't a reason to commit — which frees the decision to be about what makes a good commit.

**And there, I'd still sweep first and make it one commit.** Rule plus application, one validation run, one push. Committing the rule alone means shipping a commit whose own set violates it in ~45 places, then a second commit fixing that — two commits, two validations, and a window where `git log -- agent-data/` shows a rule nobody follows. Sweeping first costs nothing extra, since the validation has to run once either way.

**One question I can't answer for you: does `messages/test-msg.md` stay?** It's a 17-byte specimen created for the README example, currently uncommitted. If the example is to be live it has to be committed and pushed, and then it needs a rung — but it's off-topic for a commit titled "no semicolons in durable prose". Options are to give it its own trivial rung, let it ride the sweep and accept the off-topic file, or drop it and point the example at something already committed. `notes/chores/chores-07.md` is real and pushed at `a69f2d45d3d2` today, which is why your `outcome-remote` example already resolves — but pointing `local`/`remote` at a chores section would muddle what the example is showing.

So: sweep, then one commit carrying rule, sweep and whatever you decide about `test-msg.md`, then push, then the README SHAs, then the messages repo's first commit. Say go and I'll start the sweep.

content.text:
The question worth asking first is *what* would be versioned, because the two candidates have very different value here.

**A repo version-of-record has no reader.** The family scheme exists so a built artifact can answer "which commit produced me" — `iiac-perf -V`. This repo builds nothing and runs nothing, so a per-commit bump would be a number nobody can query. It would also drag in cycle machinery that doesn't fit: commits here are "added a record" and "marked read", not cycles with openings and close-outs.

**A format version has a real reader** — whoever writes a parser, or reads old records. But the format is already designed so they don't need it: "fields may be added later without breaking what is already written, a reader ignores fields it does not know, and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands." That's forward compatibility by construction, which is exactly the job a version number would otherwise do. Adding one now would be a second mechanism for a guarantee we already have, and one that needs maintaining.

**A version only becomes load-bearing on a *breaking* change** — a field renamed, or `read` changing meaning. Additive changes need nothing. And at the moment we break something we'd know it, and could stamp a version then, on evidence rather than in advance.

**So my suggestion: state the contract instead of the number.** The README currently says fields may be added but doesn't forbid renaming or repurposing them, which leaves the compatibility promise half-written. One line completes it:

```
Format changes are additive. A field is added, never renamed or repurposed, so a reader written
against an older README still reads today's records. That is why there is no format version. A
change that broke it would need one, and there has not been such a change.
```

That gives a parser author the guarantee they'd otherwise ask a version for, and it records *why* there's no version so nobody re-opens it in three months.

**And the history already answers the question a version would.** Every record is dated by its commit, the README's history shows when the format moved, so "which format was this written under" is derivable from the two. Same shape as everything else we've kept tonight — derived rather than restated.

If you want a version anyway for uniformity with the other repos, I'd put it in the README as a format version rather than a manifest, and only bump it when the contract above is broken. But I'd not bump per commit, because there is nothing to stamp and nobody to ask.
