# vc-x1-messages

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
nothing.

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1

- local: [../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1

The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.

Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
section slug.

- `local:` the message's local file reference.
- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
  unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
  both halves of an exchange.

A handled record with all of them:

## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1

- local: [[1]]
- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/messages/test-msg.md#message1
- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
- outcome-local: [[2]]
- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/a69f2d45d3d2/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push

[1]: ../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1
[2]: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#the-proposal-two-flags-on-push

**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read.

**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.

## Two modes, fast and durable

The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.

- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
  that push made resolvable.

**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.

**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
push.

## Write and commit in one act

Whoever writes a record commits it, in the same act. There is then no moment at which an
uncommitted record exists, and nobody has to remember to commit someone else's writing later.
This repo has no manager and needs none, because ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. **This one is
  a proposal rather than a settled rule**, and the first thing worth vc-x1's opinion.

## No protection

Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

content.text:
Added at the top. Four decisions folded in, each of which I'd rather have you veto than have me leave implicit:

**It versions the *format*, not the repo.** No manifest, no per-commit bump, because this repo builds nothing and nothing can be asked "what version are you". The format is the thing that changes and the thing a reader depends on.

**0.1.0 rather than 1.0.0**, because vc-x1 hasn't seen it. It says "this works and isn't agreed yet", which is the truth tonight.

**The bump scale is mapped to what a reader cares about**, following versioning.md's scope test: patch is wording and examples, minor is a field or rule added, major would break an existing reader. That makes the number informative — a minor tells you to skim for a new field, a major tells you your parser is wrong — rather than decorative.

**The additive contract rides with it**, because a version without a compatibility promise says nothing. It also states why records carry no version of their own: they don't need one, and a record's commit dates it against this file's history. That closes the question rather than leaving the next reader to re-derive it.

Two things you may want to move or cut. It sits *above* the sentence that says what the repo is, so a first-time reader meets a version before a purpose — putting it after the two-line intro would read better and is still "at the top". And the last sentence about records carrying no version is arguably a design note rather than a version note, so it could live further down if you want the header to be three lines instead of five.

# vc-x1-messages v0.1.0

Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
only pointers to them, one record per message.

**Format 0.1.0.** Changes are additive, so a field is added and never renamed or repurposed, and
a reader written against an older version still reads today's records. Patch is wording and
examples, minor is a field or a rule added, major would break an existing reader and has not
happened. A record carries no version because it does not need one, and its commit dates it
against this file's history.

To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
nothing.

a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
in a record, only the field lines are read.

**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.

## Two modes, fast and durable

The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.

- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
  that push made resolvable.

**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.

**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
nothing, and mark it read.

Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
push.

Whoever writes a record commits it, in the same act. There is then no moment at which an
uncommitted record exists, and nobody has to remember to commit someone else's writing later.
This repo has no manager and needs none, because ownership is per write rather than per repo.

## The remote reference is a commit permalink

The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
`<commit-sha>` is not optional.

- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
  message is worth reading.
- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
  this form.
- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
  the remote one.

## Each file's owner sets its persistence

A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
where to add one.

- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
  A recommendation, not a rule.
- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. **This one is
  a proposal rather than a settled rule**, and the first thing worth vc-x1's opinion.

## No protection

control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

content.text:
Five lines to three, and the reader now meets the repo's purpose before its version number.

**What I cut:** the restated `0.1.0`, and the patch/minor/major table. The scale is inferable from what's left — additive changes, major means additive stopped being true — so spelling out three tiers was saying twice what one sentence says.

**What I kept, and wouldn't cut:** that the version is the *format's* rather than the repo's, and the additive contract. Without those, `v0.1.0` in a title is decoration. With them, a parser author knows exactly what they're allowed to rely on, which is the only reason the number is worth carrying.

**The record-carries-no-version note moved** into the paragraph about how readers treat records, where it belongs — it's a fact about records, not about the repo. One home each.

Incidentally `v0.1.0` in the title is the family's own convention rather than a departure: versioning.md says `v` is a display prefix for scannability, with manifests storing the bare form. There's no manifest here, so a display use in the title is exactly the case that rule allows for.

message.content: So you want to sweep for ";"? I think we commit this with just messages/test-msg.md and a short explanation in chores and then commit/close-out this and vc-x1-message. Push back welcome!

content.text:
Push back on two of the three, and one thing has gone missing.

**On the sweep: I'd drop it from this cycle, reversing myself.** I argued for it when the cycle looked like a convergence cycle with room. It isn't any more — the evening's real output is a new repo and a protocol, and adding ~45 mechanical edits across eight files on top of that buries both. The rule in `prose.md` is the proposal, the diff carries it, and the application can be its own small cycle once vc-x1 has ruled. You argued the other way and I conceded then. The circumstance changed, not the argument.

**On closing out: it fails the acceptance check on two of three items, and they're the cycle's whole point.** The opening committed to:

1. every difference from vc-x1 accounted for with a verdict — partially met, and `prose.md` is now a third difference needing one
2. nothing surviving only in `tmp/` — met
3. `messages/vc-x1.md` carrying the early entry and the full reply — **not met at all**, nothing has been sent

The checklist allows closing on a failed check, since "a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner". What it doesn't allow is revising the check toward what we achieved, which is the tempting move here. So closing is legal if we record the failure honestly. I'd rather spend one more rung and pass it — the message is drafted, and it's the thing the whole cycle was named for.

And re-titling the cycle isn't available as an escape: the bookends must share the title, and the opening is pushed with an `ochid:` trailer, so hard rule 4 and the drafts rule both bar re-describing it.

**On the commit shape: two rungs, not one.** What's uncommitted is two unrelated problems — the semicolon rule in `prose.md`, and the messages-repo design plus `test-msg.md`. The commit-body form says a body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking to be more than one commit, and `git log -- agent-data/` reads correctly only if the rule change stands alone. Two small commits, one validation run each, and neither has to explain the other.

**What's gone missing: the drafted message doesn't mention the messages repo.** It's still the 2026-08-13 entry about duplicated cycle rules and extending `push`. The biggest thing to tell vc-x1 tonight is that a messaging repo exists, here's its README, please review — and none of that is in it. Either it becomes a third item in that message, or it's a second message, but as it stands we'd be announcing the repo to them by mentioning it in conversation and never writing it down.

**So what I'd do:** commit the two rungs, push, update the README permalinks to the new SHA, commit `vc-x1-messages`, then one more rung that delivers the message with the repo announcement in it — and close out on a passing check. If you'd rather stop tonight, then close out with item 3 recorded as failed and the review carried to its own cycle, which is honest but leaves the cycle having converged nothing.

Park it: leave the edits uncommitted in the working copy, where they seed the sweep cycle at step 7. jj holds them safely through the close-out and the land, and nothing is lost.

Consequence worth knowing: until step 7, the semicolon rule is a local uncommitted edit, so it is **not** in the diff vc-x1 reviews. We've told them the diff is our proposal set, so that proposal is invisible to them until then.

**2. The close-out has to run the acceptance check and record it failing.** It asked for every difference verdicted and the reply delivered. Neither happened — the evening went to designing a messages repo instead. The checklist allows closing on a failed check but not revising the check toward what we achieved, so it gets recorded as a finding with the carry-forward named: the formal review owed since 2026-08-08, the two answers from their 2026-08-12 message, and the drafted message itself. **3. The close-out is where the messages-repo design gets its record.** It's the cycle's largest output and currently exists only in this session. Without it, `chores-07` records a message we never sent and says nothing about the repo we built.

**4. Add the land.** After the close-out push, hard rule 13: `jj bookmark set main -r <cycle>`, `jj bookmark delete <cycle>`, `jj git push -b main -b <cycle>`. Then the as-built backfill for both commits comes due and rides the next cycle's first push.

##### docs: converge the agent-files with vc-x1 closing

**Problem: the check was called failed before it was run.** Closing was argued against on the
grounds that two of three measures would fail. Running them one at a time showed one failure, the
undelivered message, with the other two passing once the record did its ordinary job.

**Solution.** Run the measures before characterising them. The checklist says a failed check is a
finding, and a finding needs the same evidence as any other claim.

**Problem: one `cd` silently moved every later command.** A single `cd ../vc-x1-messages && sed
...` left the working directory there for the rest of the session, which produced a confidently
wrong claim that a file did not exist, a `.claude` of sandbox mounts in a repo that wants no
agent, and a `jj restore` that resolved its path against the wrong root.

**Solution.** The working practice already says it. Stay in the project root and reach elsewhere
with `-R` or an absolute path. The cost of breaking it is not the one command, it is every command
after it.

#### Design: the vc-x1-messages repo

A shared repo for family correspondence, built this cycle and unreviewed by anyone else. The
protocol lives in its own `README.md` at format 0.1.0. What is recorded here is what was decided
and why, since the README states the rules without the alternatives they beat.

- **Why a repo at all.** Mailboxes live in the template repository, whose `main` is a single
  `Initial commit` with everything else uncommitted, so a handled message deleted there is
  unrecoverable. `custom-family.md`'s copy-into-chores-before-deleting rule exists only to
  compensate for that.
- **Plain, with no agent, and the reason is structural rather than taste.** A managed repo
  inherits "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent", which is the rule that
  created mailboxes in the first place, so a manager would make the one repo everyone must write
  to writable by one member. What replaces the manager is a rule: whoever writes a record commits
  it, in the same act.
- **Bodies stay in the sender's repo and only pointers live in the shared one.** That is what
  makes a notification record losable without loss, which in turn is what lets each file's owner
  choose their own persistence policy without endangering anything.
- **Records, not a positional line.** The line format was revised four times in about an hour,
  which is a format asking to become named fields. A `##` heading gives each record an anchor for
  free, so a reply can cite an exact entry with no invented id.
- **The remote reference is a commit permalink**, since a branch name rots exactly when the
  message becomes worth reading: a topic bookmark is deleted at landing and the permanent branch
  does not carry the file until then. That creates an ordering constraint the README now states,
  because a permalink cannot be written before the commit it names is pushed.
- **Strict for writers, tolerant for readers.** A malformed record is not an error, with one
  exception: the `##` heading must exist, because orphaned field lines join the record above, so
  an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
- **Deliberately unsolved: notification.** No file in any repo can reach someone who is not
  looking. GitHub issues would, at the cost of moving correspondence outside the clone, the diff
  and jj history, so they are held in reserve for that one job.
- **Open for vc-x1**: whether a member's file may be created by whoever writes first, which is
  what a first message to a new member requires and which the README carries as a proposal rather
  than a rule.

39	  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |

54	  being the same rung written twice.

56	  drops the restatement and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and
57	  the trapezoid recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.

59	  rather than two. We could find no written case for keeping them separate, which is what the

61

63	
64	Making one or more already-pushed commits permanent, with `<branch>` the bookmark that advances
65	and `<cycle>` the topic bookmark it advances to. Measured 2026-08-13 in a throwaway repo pair built
66	to that premise.
67	
68	```
69	jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>' -R .        # precondition; empty output means <branch> moved, stop
70	jj bookmark set <branch> -r <cycle> -R .  # local
71	jj bookmark delete <cycle> -R .           # local
72	jj git push -b <branch> -b <cycle> -R .   # one push, both halves
73	```
74	
75	- **Three commands, not four.** A deletion needs no push of its own: `-b` repeats, and naming a
76	  locally deleted bookmark publishes its deletion. Bare `jj git push` is not a substitute, since it
77	  declines to publish deletions without `--deleted` or an explicit `-b`.

87	  left dangling.

91	`vc-x1 push --from <cycle> --to <branch> --delete-from` (wink, 2026-08-13), superseding a
92	`vc-x1 land` subcommand drafted first. The margin is too thin for a new verb: `push` already
93	commits both repos, advances the destination bookmark and publishes it, measured by
94	`vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` running four of its five stages.
95	
96	Three flags, one of them a rename:
97	
98	- **`--to <branch>`**, the bookmark that advances, renaming `push`'s existing `[BOOKMARK]`
99	  positional / `--bookmark` rather than adding an argument. The positional stays as shorthand.
100	- **`--from <cycle>`**, the bookmark it advances to. Safety and cleanup only, never content
101	  selection: `bookmark-set` hardcodes `-r @-`, so what publishes is always where you stand.

# message1
Hello
=== design section:
A shared repo for family correspondence, built this cycle and unreviewed by anyone else. The
protocol lives in its own `README.md` at format 0.1.0. What is recorded here is what was decided
and why, since the README states the rules without the alternatives they beat.

- **Why a repo at all.** Mailboxes live in the template repository, whose `main` is a single
  `Initial commit` with everything else uncommitted, so a handled message deleted there is
  unrecoverable. `custom-family.md`'s copy-into-chores-before-deleting rule exists only to
  compensate for that.
- **Plain, with no agent, and the reason is structural rather than taste.** A managed repo
  inherits "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent", which is the rule that
  created mailboxes in the first place, so a manager would make the one repo everyone must write
  to writable by one member. What replaces the manager is a rule: whoever writes a record commits
  it, in the same act.
- **Bodies stay in the sender's repo and only pointers live in the shared one.** That is what
  makes a notification record losable without loss, which in turn is what lets each file's owner
  choose their own persistence policy without endangering anything.
- **Records, not a positional line.** The line format was revised four times in about an hour,
  which is a format asking to become named fields. A `##` heading gives each record an anchor for
  free, so a reply can cite an exact entry with no invented id.
- **The remote reference is a commit permalink**, since a branch name rots exactly when the
  message becomes worth reading: a topic bookmark is deleted at landing and the permanent branch
  does not carry the file until then. That creates an ordering constraint the README now states,
  because a permalink cannot be written before the commit it names is pushed.
- **Strict for writers, tolerant for readers.** A malformed record is not an error, with one
  exception: the `##` heading must exist, because orphaned field lines join the record above, so
  an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
- **Deliberately unsolved: notification.** No file in any repo can reach someone who is not
  looking. GitHub issues would, at the cost of moving correspondence outside the clone, the diff
  and jj history, so they are held in reserve for that one job.
- **Open for vc-x1**: whether a member's file may be created by whoever writes first, which is
  what a first message to a new member requires and which the README carries as a proposal rather
  than a rule.

## docs: design the vc-x1-messages repo

- [[N]] docs: design the vc-x1-messages repo

A shared repo for family correspondence, built in one sitting and unreviewed by anyone else. The
protocol lives in its own `README.md` at format 0.1.0, and this project's inbox is `iiac-perf.md`
beside it. What is recorded here is what was decided and why, since the README states the rules
without the alternatives they beat.

The repo exists because the transport was the defect rather than the messages riding it. That
diagnosis came out of a day spent finding that everything owed to another member was sitting in a
gitignored scratch file, with no durable place to put it.

- **Why a repo at all.** Mailboxes live in the template repository, whose `main` is a single
  `Initial commit` with everything else uncommitted, so a handled message deleted there is
  unrecoverable. `custom-family.md`'s copy-into-chores-before-deleting rule exists only to
  compensate for that.
- **Plain, with no agent, and the reason is structural rather than taste.** A managed repo
  inherits "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent", which is the rule that
  created mailboxes in the first place, so a manager would make the one repo everyone must write
  to writable by one member. What replaces the manager is a rule: whoever writes a record commits
  it, in the same act.
- **Bodies stay in the sender's repo and only pointers live in the shared one.** That is what
  makes a notification record losable without loss, which in turn is what lets each file's owner
  choose their own persistence policy without endangering anything.
- **Records, not a positional line.** The line format was revised four times in about an hour,
  which is a format asking to become named fields. A `##` heading gives each record an anchor for
  free, so a reply can cite an exact entry with no invented id.
- **The remote reference is a commit permalink**, since a branch name rots exactly when the
  message becomes worth reading: a topic bookmark is deleted at landing and the permanent branch
  does not carry the file until then. That creates an ordering constraint the README now states,
  because a permalink cannot be written before the commit it names is pushed.
- **Strict for writers, tolerant for readers.** A malformed record is not an error, with one
  exception: the `##` heading must exist, because orphaned field lines join the record above, so
  an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
- **Deliberately unsolved: notification.** No file in any repo can reach someone who is not
  looking. GitHub issues would, at the cost of moving correspondence outside the clone, the diff
  and jj history, so they are held in reserve for that one job.
- **Open for vc-x1**: whether a member's file may be created by whoever writes first, which is
  what a first message to a new member requires and which the README carries as a proposal rather
  than a rule.

### The specimen is the point of `messages/test-msg.md`

The one file this cycle adds to this repo is a two-line message. It exists so the README's
examples reference something real: a `local` path that resolves in a sibling clone and a `remote`
permalink that resolves for a reader with none.

**It also proves the ordering rule by needing it.** The README's permalinks pointed at a commit
that did not contain this file, so they answered 404 until it was committed and pushed. The rule
was written from that failure rather than in anticipation of it.

### Where this leaves the messages repo

`vc-x1-messages` is committed separately and is not part of this repo's history. This section is
the durable record of the reasoning, reachable from this commit's `ochid:` trailer, because a
plain repo has no agent repo of its own and its commits carry no trailer.

Still owed and deliberately not in this cycle: telling vc-x1 the repo exists, their review of it,
and whatever the review changes.

_None yet._

input.content:
Family members leave word for each other in mailboxes that cannot
keep it. They live in a repo whose main is a single initial commit
with everything else uncommitted, so a handled message deleted
there is unrecoverable, and the rule that copies a message into
chores before deleting it exists only to compensate for that. The
transport is the defect, not the messages riding it.

* A shared store fixes durability only if writing to it cannot be
  postponed, and only if nobody has to own it.
- vc-x1-messages is a plain repo with no agent, where whoever
  writes a record commits it in the same act. A managed repo would
  inherit the rule that gives one agent sole write access, which is
  the opposite of what correspondence needs.
* Anything a shared store holds alone can be destroyed by whoever
  curates it.
- Bodies stay in the sender's own repo and only pointers are
  shared, so a notification can be lost without loss and each
  file's owner may choose their own persistence policy safely.
* A pointer is worth nothing if it stops resolving.
- References are commit permalinks, since a branch name rots
  exactly when the message becomes worth reading. The specimen
  message added here is what the format's examples point at, and
  its absence from an earlier commit is what taught the ordering
  the README now states.

There's a real data point in the joke, though. 1	# vc-x1-messages v0.1.0
2	
3	Notifications for the vc-x1 family. Message bodies live in the sender's own repo, this repo holds
4	only pointers to them, one record per message.
5	
6	The version above is the record format's, and changes to it are additive. A field is added, never
7	renamed or repurposed, so a reader written against an older version still reads today's records.
8	A major bump would mean that stopped being true and there has not been one.
9	
10	To send a message create a file with the message and a markdown section header somewhere in your
11	repo. Then add a record to the file named for the destination you find here, directly below that
12	file's own header, so the newest record is first. Whether a push sits between those two steps is
13	[the choice of mode](#two-modes-fast-and-durable) below. A record is a `##` heading and a list of
14	fields and each field is generally "owned" by the creator, although fixing errors is
15	permissible. Every field is optional and records routinely carry only two or three, though a
16	writer aims for at least one of `local` or `remote`, since a record with neither points at
17	nothing.
18	
19	## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1
20	
21	- local: [../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1](../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1)
22	- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/messages/test-msg.md#message1
23	
24	The heading is `<utc-timestamp> <sender>`. It is also the record's anchor, so a reply or a
25	record elsewhere can link at this exact entry without anyone inventing an id.
26	
27	Then a dash list of `- field: <value>`, where every reference may carry an optional markdown
28	section slug.
29	
30	- `local:` the message's local file reference.
31	- `remote:` the message's remote file reference.
32	- `read:` added by the recipient, a UTC timestamp of when they read it. A record without it is
33	  unread, so a member's open traffic is the records in their file with no `read` field.
34	- `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` optional, added by the recipient, pointing at what came of
35	  the message, the reply or the record of what was decided. They are what let one record hold
36	  both halves of an exchange.
37	
38	A handled record with all of them:
39	
40	## 2026-08-13T19:31:21.123Z vc-x1
41	
42	- local: [[1]]
43	- remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/messages/test-msg.md#message1
44	- read: 2026-08-13T22:04:07.000Z
45	- outcome-local: [[2]]
46	- outcome-remote: https://github.com/winksaville/iiac-perf/blob/55554b452957/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo
47	
48	[1]: ../iiac-perf/messages/test-msg.md#message1
49	[2]: ../iiac-perf/notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo
50	
51	**Fields may be added later without breaking what is already written**, which is why a record is
52	a list of named fields rather than a positional line. A reader ignores fields it does not know,
53	and a record missing an optional field is complete as it stands. Prose may sit beside the fields
54	in a record, only the field lines are read. A record carries no version of its own, since its
55	commit dates it against this file's history.
56	
57	**A malformed record is not an error, only less useful**, and a reader takes what is there rather
58	than rejecting it. A heading that lost its sender is even recoverable, since whoever wrote a
59	record committed it. The one part that must be present is the `##` heading itself, because it is
60	what separates one record from the next. Field lines with no heading above them are read as part
61	of the record before, so an interrupted write damages its neighbour rather than itself.
62	
63	## Two modes, fast and durable
64	
65	The message file lives in your repo either way. What differs is whether the record carries a
66	permalink, and that decides both the order of the steps and how long the record stays good for.
67	
68	- **Fast, local only.** Write the message file, add the record with `local` alone, done. No push
69	  and no waiting, and the reader resolves it from their sibling clone.
70	- **Durable.** Write the message file, commit and push it, then add the record with the `remote`
71	  that push made resolvable.
72	
73	**The order matters only in the durable mode, and it is the step people miss.** A permalink names
74	a commit, so it cannot be written before that commit exists and is pushed. Write the record first
75	and you have a URL that 404s until the file catches up with it.
76	
77	**Write a record once, when you have what goes in it.** Writing it early with an empty `remote`
78	costs two writes to this repo for one message, and a reader may follow the empty one, find
79	nothing, and mark it read.
80	
81	Which mode to use is the tradeoff in
82	[The remote reference is a commit permalink](#the-remote-reference-is-a-commit-permalink) below.
83	Same-day traffic between siblings is fine on local alone. Anything worth citing later wants the
84	push.
85	
86	## Write and commit in one act
87	
88	Whoever writes a record commits it, in the same act. There is then no moment at which an
89	uncommitted record exists, and nobody has to remember to commit someone else's writing later.
90	This repo has no manager and needs none, because ownership is per write rather than per repo.
91	
92	## The remote reference is a commit permalink
93	
94	The remote form is `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<commit-sha>/<path>#<slug>`, and the
95	`<commit-sha>` is not optional.
96	
97	- **A branch name rots.** A topic bookmark is deleted once its cycle lands, and the permanent
98	  branch does not carry the file until then, so both forms break at exactly the moment the
99	  message is worth reading.
100	- **A commit SHA does not.** It survives the bookmark's deletion, survives a rebase of anything
101	  after it, and resolves for a reader with no clone. GitHub's `y` key converts a branch URL into
102	  this form.
103	- **The local form names a path, the remote form names a version.** A local reference resolves to
104	  whatever that file says now, in whatever state that working copy happens to be, and it assumes
105	  the member repos are siblings of this one. A remote reference resolves to what was actually
106	  sent. Local-only is fine for traffic read the same day, anything meant to be read later wants
107	  the remote one.
108	
109	## Each file's owner sets its persistence
110	
111	A member's file belongs to whoever receives on it. They create it, they curate it, and they
112	declare at its head what becomes of a handled record. A sender needs to know none of that, only
113	where to add one.
114	
115	- **Marking beats deleting, and the reason is the sender.** Whether a message was read is
116	  recorded nowhere else, not in the sender's repo and not in the reader's, so a policy that marks
117	  a handled record tells the sender it arrived while one that deletes it tells them nothing.
118	  A recommendation, not a rule.
119	- **Nothing worth keeping is ever only here.** The body is a committed file in the sender's repo,
120	  and that commit carries the `ochid:` trailer linking the session that wrote it. A notification
121	  record can be lost without losing anything, which is what makes owner-chosen policies safe.
122	- **A file that does not exist yet is created by whoever writes first**, carrying no policy until
123	  its owner declares one. Reserving creation to the owner would make the first message to a new
124	  member impossible, since only the owner may create and only the sender wants to. **This one is
125	  a proposal rather than a settled rule**, and the first thing worth vc-x1's opinion.
126	
127	## No protection
128	
129	Any member can modify or delete any file here. This is a cooperative store with no access
130	control, so it works only among friendly participants and history is the only recourse.

input.content:
The vc-x1 family has no durable place to leave word for each other.
Mailboxes live in a repo whose main is a single initial commit with
everything else uncommitted, so a handled message deleted there is
unrecoverable, and the rule that copies a message into chores before
deleting it exists only to compensate.

- This repo holds notifications only. Message bodies stay in the
  sender's own repo, so a record here can be lost without losing
  anything, which is what lets each file's owner decide how their
  own file is kept.
- Whoever writes a record commits it in the same act. That is what
  a plain repo has instead of a manager, and a manager would make
  the one repo everyone must write to writable by one member.
- iiac-perf.md is the first inbox and declares its own policy at
  its head.

Format 0.1.0, unreviewed by the rest of the family. The reasoning
behind each rule is recorded in iiac-perf's chores-07.
